notes.explains: In a 15-minute game, Black plays a Modern Defense with g6, and White responds with a flank pawn push h4. The principle is to meet h4 with h5 to stop White's expansion, but Black instead plays d5, allowing White to continue with g4.
notes.teaches: When your opponent pushes a flank pawn like h4, immediately challenging it with h5 can neutralize their space-gaining attempt.
notes.plans: Black should consider h5 to prevent White's pawn storm, or if already played d5, be ready to meet g4 with Bxg4.

notes.explains: After White plays g4, Black misses the tactical opportunity Bxg4, which would win a pawn. Instead, Black plays f6, a weakening move that allows White to strike in the center with e4, gaining initiative.
notes.teaches: When a pawn is offered, always consider if you can safely capture it, especially if it opens lines or wins material. Avoid weakening pawn moves like f6 without a clear purpose.
notes.plans: Black should have taken on g4 and then aimed to develop pieces and castle quickly.

notes.explains: When the opponent threatens to capture a piece, you might be tempted to play a move like d4 to create a fork, but if it allows a capture with check, it's often not good. Instead, consider castling to safety first.
notes.teaches: Don't rush into tactical tricks if they leave you vulnerable. Sometimes the principled move, like castling, is better than a flashy fork that backfires.
notes.plans: Castle to get the king safe, then continue development and address the tension later.

notes.explains: White's move a3 is harmless and gives you space on the queenside. You can continue with a5 to prevent b4, but even if you don't, it's not a big deal. However, there is a tactical trick: the pawn on d6 is only protected by the knight on f6, so White could play b5 to attack the knight and win the pawn.
notes.teaches: Always be alert to tactical opportunities in the opening, especially when a pawn is only defended once. Also, moves like a3 can be harmless and give the opponent space.
notes.plans: Consider playing a5 to stop b4, and be careful to keep your pawns protected.

notes.explains: After Black plays c5, if White ever plays d4, the bishop on c5 would be hanging. Black can also consider an immediate Nd4, which attacks two points and offers a favorable transformation: if White takes, Black recaptures with the pawn and forks; if the bishop takes, Black gains the bishop pair.
notes.teaches: Look for tactical tricks that exploit the opponent's pawn breaks, and be willing to trade a knight for a bishop to secure the bishop pair.
notes.plans: Consider Nd4 to create threats and force a favorable exchange, or maintain the tension to keep pressure on d4.

notes.explains: When Black plays Bf5 in the Scandinavian, White can respond with Qf3, attacking the bishop and potentially creating threats. This is a tactical resource that punishes early bishop development.
notes.teaches: Look for moves that combine attack and development, especially targeting loose pieces.
notes.plans: If Black's bishop is misplaced, use queen moves to gain tempo and pressure.

notes.explains: In this game, the opponent's lack of opening principles led to a blunder that allowed a queen and bishop battery to win a piece. The opponent's 'freestyling' was punished by sound play.
notes.teaches: If you follow opening principles, you will often get chances to punish opponents who ignore them. Look for tactical opportunities like batteries and forks.
notes.plans: After winning material, continue developing and consolidate your advantage by trading pieces and simplifying.

notes.explains: Black played ...c5, which hangs multiple pawns (on b6, d5, and e5 after captures). This is a tactical blunder that loses material.
notes.teaches: Before making a pawn move, check if it leaves other pawns undefended. Keep your pawns protected like a fence; don't knock down posts.
notes.plans: After ...c5, White should capture the hanging pawns and maintain the material advantage.

notes.explains: In the Scandinavian, a common tactical trick occurs when White plays Bg5, pinning the knight on c6 to the queen. However, the knight is defended by the queen, so the pin is illusory: Black can simply take the knight with the queen, winning a piece.
notes.teaches: Always check if a pinned piece is actually defended. In the Scandinavian, the queen on c7 defends the knight, so Bg5 is a blunder that loses the bishop.
notes.plans: If White plays Bg5, capture the knight with the queen, winning a piece. Otherwise, continue with normal development.

notes.explains: When an opponent attacks with a lone knight early, it often lacks a concrete threat. If you can capture a pawn or piece that was previously defended, you punish the premature attack.
notes.teaches: Be alert to the fact that pieces that move away leave behind undefended squares or pawns. Exploit such weaknesses by capturing them.
notes.plans: After punishing the early knight move, continue developing your pieces and aim to castle quickly.

notes.explains: Black trades off a light-squared bishop on f3, which is a mistake because Black has many pawns on dark squares and needs the light-squared bishop to defend them. After the trade, Black's pawn structure is weak, and White's pieces become more active.
notes.teaches: When your pawns are fixed on one color, keep the bishop that controls the opposite color. Trading it can leave you with a bad bishop and weaknesses.
notes.plans: Black should avoid such trades and instead try to develop and castle. White can exploit the weakened dark squares and the hanging b7 pawn.

notes.explains: After a bad trade by the opponent, the quality of the remaining pieces matters. A light-squared bishop that is blocked by its own pawns is bad, while the opponent's bishop has prospects. A move like g6 can limit the enemy knight's activity.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, identify the worst-placed piece and improve it. Use pawn moves to restrict enemy pieces, and look for targets on the outskirts of the enemy king's position.
notes.plans: Reposition your pieces to target weak points, such as the pawns around the enemy king. Once you win one pawn, you can often come back for more.

notes.explains: Black plays Nxd4, hoping to win a pawn after Bxd4, but the pawn isn't free because b7 is hanging and White can develop with tempo, e.g., Rd1. Black's position remains under pressure.
notes.teaches: Before grabbing a pawn, check if it is truly free or if it comes with tactical drawbacks like hanging pieces or development issues.
notes.plans: White should continue to pressure Black's weaknesses and complete development. Black needs to consolidate and find a way to develop the queenside.

notes.explains: A pawn grab that seems to win a free pawn can be illusory if it leaves other weaknesses or allows the opponent to activate their pieces. Here, the pawn is not truly free because of hanging pieces and tactical threats.
notes.teaches: Before taking a 'free' pawn, check if it is truly safe and if it allows your opponent to gain compensation or launch an attack.

notes.explains: The opponent plays knight f4, which is a tactical mistake because two of my pieces are looking at that square. If they take with the bishop, I can take with the rook, and the opponent loses their queen.
notes.teaches: When you have multiple pieces attacking a square, a piece landing there can be a tactical blunder if it's not adequately defended. Always count attackers and defenders before moving a piece to a contested square.
notes.plans: Take the knight with the bishop, and if the opponent recaptures, take with the rook to win the queen.

notes.explains: When the opponent's pieces are deep in your position, they may leave weaknesses behind. For example, a knight that blocks a check might stop defending a bishop or a pawn. The opponent's king may be far from castling, and their pieces may be attacking without a clear plan.
notes.teaches: When your opponent invades your position, look for tactical resources like checks and counterattacks. Also, notice when their pieces are overloaded—defending multiple things at once. If you can create threats that force them to move, you may win material.
notes.plans: Continue to create threats and exploit the opponent's lack of coordination. Look for ways to win the hanging pawn or bishop.

notes.explains: There is a hidden tactic involving knight takes, knight takes, queen takes, leading to a queen trade. This shows the importance of tactical awareness even in quiet positions.
notes.teaches: Always look for tactical sequences, especially when pieces are aligned. Doing puzzles helps spot these patterns.
notes.plans: If the tactic appears, consider trading queens to simplify into a favorable endgame with an extra pawn.

notes.explains: When queens are separated by just one piece, and the queen is unprotected, there is often a tactic. In this case, a sequence of captures leads to winning the queen. The tactic is visible if you calculate the capture chain.
notes.teaches: Always be alert for one-move and two-move tactics, especially when the enemy queen is undefended and only a piece away from your queen. Also, you must see such tactics from a distance, both for yourself and to avoid falling into them.
notes.plans: If you spot such a tactic, calculate it fully before playing. If you are the defender, avoid leaving your queen vulnerable in that way.

notes.explains: In this position, a check is available that also attacks a knight. This is a classic example of using checks, captures, and attacks to find the best move.
notes.teaches: Always look for checks, captures, and attacks first. This checklist can reveal strong moves that win material or create threats.
notes.plans: Deliver the check, and when the opponent blocks, capture the attacked knight.

notes.explains: The opponent made a mistake by moving a piece that was protecting their bishop, leaving the bishop hanging. This is a common tactical oversight.
notes.teaches: Always check what pieces are protecting each other. Moving a defender can leave other pieces en prise.
notes.plans: Capture the hanging bishop and continue to press.

notes.explains: In a winning position, you can consider tactical shots like sacrificing the queen for two rooks or delivering a double check. These are fun but not necessary; simple moves also win.
notes.teaches: Tactical opportunities arise from superior piece activity. Even if you miss a brilliant move, you can still win by playing sound chess.
notes.plans: Choose the most forcing and safe continuation to finish the game.

notes.explains: In this position, a tactical combination was available: Rg8+ followed by Be8, which would win material. However, the safer move Be8 was chosen because it completely paralyzes the opponent without risking a sacrifice.
notes.teaches: When a sacrifice wins, but a quiet move achieves the same or better result without risk, prefer the quiet move. Look for moves that restrict the opponent's pieces entirely.
notes.plans: Play Be8 to lock down the position, then continue pushing the g-pawn. Avoid the rook sacrifice because the opponent's king can defend the bishop, making the tactic fail.

notes.explains: The move g4 by the opponent is a sign of desperation, as it weakens their pawn structure and creates tactical opportunities. The player spots that rook d4 is a fork, winning the knight, and that taking the pawn is not necessary.
notes.teaches: When your opponent makes a pawn move like g4, look for tactics that exploit the weaknesses created. You don't always have to take back; sometimes you can ignore a capture to play a stronger move.
notes.plans: Play rook e8 to attack the pawn on e7, and be ready to use tactics like rook d4 to win material if the opponent tries to create counterplay.

notes.explains: The attacking side has multiple mating threats, but the defender can survive by finding a specific defensive resource, such as a check that forces a draw. The position is razor-thin: one move wins, another draws, and another loses.
notes.teaches: In sharp positions, every move must be checked for tactical consequences. A move that is not a check or a threat can allow the opponent to escape or even turn the tables.
notes.plans: If you are defending, look for checks and counter-threats that can force a repetition or a trade of pieces to reach a draw.

notes.explains: White plays Bg5, mirroring the bishop on g5, which is a common but not always best approach. The position has tactical possibilities, such as the idea of Ne4, hitting the bishop and creating threats.
notes.teaches: Look for moves that create multiple threats or target pieces that are only defended once. Even in quiet positions, tactical motifs like forks and pins can arise.
notes.plans: Black should consider moves like h6, a6, or Qa5 to break the pin or create counterplay. White should be alert to tactical opportunities like Ne4.

notes.explains: After a trade, the rook may end up attacking the knight, which is an unfortunate side effect. The knight is hanging but cannot be taken because of tactical reasons.
notes.teaches: When a piece is attacked, look for tactical resources that prevent capture, such as counter-attacks or pins.
notes.plans: Continue offering a queen trade to maintain the advantage. If the opponent avoids it, they must move the queen, allowing the knight to escape.

notes.explains: In this position, a flashy rook sacrifice looks appealing but is not flawless; the king can escape. The real resource is a quiet bishop move that hits the knight because the queen is aligned with it, made possible by piece coordination.
notes.teaches: Before committing to a spectacular sacrifice, look for forcing moves that exploit hidden tactical motifs like pins or discovered attacks. A move that seems impossible can be possible when you see how all pieces coordinate.
notes.plans: Consider the forcing pawn move c4, which after queen takes allows rook c8, or the bishop takes pawn idea that wins material back immediately.

notes.explains: The defender has organized pieces to try to play e5, a central break that would give counterplay. The attacker notes that if the defender plays ...Re8, there is a tactical refutation involving a knight move that traps the queen.
notes.teaches: When the opponent is trying to organize a freeing break, look for tactical ways to punish the preparatory moves. Sometimes a single move can refute the entire plan.
notes.plans: If ...Re8, play Ng5 (or similar) to trap the queen and win material or force resignation.

notes.explains: Black has a tactical opportunity to win a pawn: either Nxd4 or Bxf3 followed by Nxd4. However, the instructor chooses to castle first, giving the opponent a chance to castle as well. This is a strategic choice to play principled chess and avoid early complications, even if it means missing an immediate material gain.
notes.teaches: Sometimes it's better to prioritize development and safety over winning a pawn. If you have a tactical chance, you can delay it to maintain a solid position, especially if the opponent might make a mistake later.
notes.plans: Castle kingside, then reassess the position. If the opponent fails to castle, punish them with the tactical pawn win. If they do castle, continue with a sound middlegame plan.

notes.explains: In this position, Black threatens to capture a pawn with the knight, and White's tempting pawn-to-d4 fork fails tactically because Black can capture the knight on f3 with check, forcing White to recapture with the queen and end up down two pawns.
notes.teaches: Before playing a tactical fork, always check if the opponent has an in-between move (like a capture with check) that refutes it. Material is not the only factor; initiative and development matter.
notes.plans: Instead of the flawed d4, White should rely on their lead in development to create active play, bringing pieces out and centralizing rooks.

notes.explains: A single move can remove a key defender, leaving pieces undefended and creating tactical opportunities.
notes.teaches: Always check what each move defends; if a defender is deflected, look for tactics against the now-vulnerable pieces.
notes.plans: Look for moves like bishop e5 or rook e5 that exploit the weakened defense.

notes.explains: In a position with loose pieces, a tactic exists: bishop takes e5, and if pawn recaptures, the queen is taken because the queen defends the rook. This wins material due to the unprotected rook.
notes.teaches: Look for tactics where a piece sacrifice on a square like e5 deflects the defender of another piece. Recognize 'loose pieces drop off' (LPDO) and exploit hanging pieces.
notes.plans: If the tactic is not spotted, continue with normal moves, but be alert to such tactical opportunities in the game.

notes.explains: When considering a move like queen to g4, you must first check if the opponent has a forcing reply, such as a check that wins material or disrupts your plan. Here, the queen on g4 would be too slow because the opponent can capture on d2 with check.
notes.teaches: Always look for your opponent's most forcing responses before committing to a move. If your intended move allows a dangerous check or capture, find a more resilient alternative.
notes.plans: Choose moves that maintain flexibility and avoid giving the opponent tactical opportunities. Consider prophylactic moves that address the opponent's threats.

notes.explains: A tactical opportunity arose when the opponent's knight move blocked the communication between their queen and a pawn, allowing a fork that wins material.
notes.teaches: Always be alert for tactics that arise from the opponent's pieces interfering with each other's coordination.
notes.plans: When you spot a tactical shot, calculate the consequences carefully and execute if it wins material or gives a decisive advantage.

notes.explains: The opponent creates a discovered attack on the knight, but the player can simply take the pawn because the opponent's queen is also under attack, making the knight safe.
notes.teaches: When your piece is attacked, look for counterattacks or tactical resources that neutralize the threat, such as attacking a more valuable piece.
notes.plans: After taking the pawn, the opponent must move their queen, allowing the knight to escape or reposition.

notes.explains: The opponent leaves a pawn hanging, and the player sets a trap by allowing the pawn to be taken, because there is a check that wins the queen.
notes.teaches: Always look for checks, especially when your pieces are attacked. A check can create a tactical opportunity to win material.
notes.plans: After the opponent takes the pawn, deliver the check and win the queen, gaining a decisive advantage.

notes.explains: In a winning position, look for tactical opportunities like forks and mating nets to finish the game decisively.
notes.teaches: Always be alert for checks that create forks or other tactics; they can win material or even the game.
notes.plans: Execute the fork to win the rook, then use the material advantage to convert the win.

notes.explains: The opponent's pieces are misplaced on the edge, leaving key pawns undefended. A simple sequence of captures (like a sushi chef) can win material because the opponent's pieces are out of play.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's pieces are offside, look for tactical blows to win material. Active rooks on central files support such tactics.
notes.plans: Capture the undefended pawns, using the rook to pressure the opponent's position and maintain the initiative.

notes.explains: Setting up a tactic with rook, queen, and king can lead to a decisive fork. For example, a knight move to b5 can win the queen if the opponent is forced to trade, and if they don't, the queen has no safe squares.
notes.teaches: Create tactical motifs by coordinating your pieces. Look for forks and discovered attacks that exploit the opponent's lack of coordination.
notes.plans: Execute the tactic to win the queen, then convert the material advantage by either trading into a winning endgame or delivering a direct mate.

notes.explains: A tactical sequence occurs: the opponent plays Nb4, but the player can trade queens or jump behind the queen with a knight, winning material. The opponent later puts king and queen on the same line, allowing a skewer with Bb4.
notes.teaches: In tactical positions, look for ways to exploit the opponent's king and queen alignment, and be willing to trade queens if it leads to a winning endgame.
notes.plans: If you see a tactic like Bb4 winning the queen, take it. Otherwise, you still have an extra rook and should consolidate.

notes.explains: After a sequence of pawn captures, Black notices that White could pin with Rook to a5, a high-level defensive resource. Black tests whether the opponent sees it.
notes.teaches: Before simplifying, look for tactical resources like pins that could refute the natural capture sequence.
notes.plans: If White misses the pin, Black proceeds with the capture and exploits the opening position.

notes.explains: White, after Black's blunder, has a winning move like Qxa7 or b5, but instead trades queens, repeating the same mistake. Later, White plays a knight move that loses material because of a tactic.
notes.teaches: When you have a winning tactic, execute it. Don't get distracted by other ideas. Also, be aware of tactical motifs like bishop takes h2, which can win material.
notes.plans: White should have played the immediate winning move, and after the mistake, should focus on minimizing losses and regrouping.

notes.explains: After a sequence of blunders, the dust settles and a middlegame begins; a knight on d4 attacks the rook, and a tactical sequence can win a piece.
notes.teaches: In a tactical sequence, a knight and bishop are often better than a rook, and converting an extra piece is a straightforward endgame.
notes.plans: If the opponent blunders, take the piece and simplify to a winning endgame.

notes.explains: White's move KE2 was a blunder because Black could play ...Nxe4, utilizing a pin. If White recaptures, Black has a zwischenzug that wins material.
notes.teaches: Always be alert to tactical motifs like pins and zwischenzugs. A move that seems natural can be punished by a precise tactical sequence.
notes.plans: White must avoid such blunders by calculating carefully. In this case, White should have chosen a safer move, perhaps maintaining the pin or addressing the threat.

notes.explains: White plays d4, which appears to lose a pawn to rook takes d4, but it is a tactical idea to open lines and create counterplay. Black must be careful not to fall for it.
notes.teaches: In difficult positions, look for moves that create threats or open lines, even if they seem to lose material. Always consider your opponent's best reply before committing.
notes.plans: White hopes to use the open d-file and the knight on b5 to create threats against the black king.

notes.explains: Black repeatedly misses the winning move bishop g7, which would win the queen. Instead, Black gives checks that allow White to escape and even turn the tables.
notes.teaches: When you have a winning tactic, take your time to find it. Don't settle for checks that don't improve your position; look for the most forcing and decisive continuation.
notes.plans: Identify the best tactical resource (like bishop g7) and play it immediately to win material.

notes.explains: When your opponent's queen is protecting a piece, be alert to tactical opportunities: if the queen moves, it might walk into a discovered attack or a line of fire from your rook.
notes.teaches: Always check if the opponent's pieces are overloaded or if moving them creates tactical weaknesses. Look for moves that force the opponent into uncomfortable positions.
notes.plans: If the opponent doesn't see the tactic, you can win material. If they do, you still have a good position.

notes.explains: When the opponent makes a move that looks aggressive but is actually a mistake, you can punish it by attacking the queen first, then taking the hanging bishop and pawn. This sequence wins back material and equalizes.
notes.teaches: In tactics, prioritize attacking the most valuable piece (queen) to gain tempo, then collect material; look for forcing sequences that exploit the opponent's overextension.
notes.plans: Play rook to a file to attack the queen, then capture the bishop and pawn, leaving the position equal.

notes.explains: In a tense position with a pinned rook, black found a move that maintained equality. Later, a long move like Rxe5 was necessary to convert the advantage, but spotting such moves is difficult.
notes.teaches: Long moves are often the hardest to spot. In complex positions, look for unexpected captures or checks that may be far from the current action.
notes.plans: Look for tactical shots like Rxe5 to exploit the opponent's king safety.

notes.explains: The opponent made a tactical mistake by taking with the rook, leading to a sequence that lost a piece. Even though the opponent defended well earlier, one blunder cost the game.
notes.teaches: Always check for tactical threats before capturing. A single move can turn a good position into a lost one.
notes.plans: If the opponent blunders, take advantage and convert the material advantage with careful play.

notes.explains: The opponent, down material, seeks counterplay by attacking a pawn, but this allows a tactical refutation: if the pawn is taken, a discovered attack wins the rook. The correct response is to take the rook rather than the knight, maximizing material gain.
notes.teaches: When your opponent creates counterplay, look for tactical shots that punish their aggression, especially those that win more material or expose their king.
notes.plans: Take the rook, then consolidate by defending against any threats and continuing to improve your pieces.

notes.explains: In this position, Black had a tactical opportunity to play a knight sacrifice on f2, winning a pawn and attacking the rook, with no counterplay for White. This would leave Black up a pawn. The player missed this tactic during the game.
notes.teaches: Always look for tactical shots, especially when pieces are hanging or when a sacrifice can win material or create a strong attack. Even simple tactics like a knight fork on f2 can be decisive.
notes.plans: When a tactic is available, calculate it carefully and take it if it leads to a clear advantage, such as winning a pawn and attacking a rook.

notes.explains: A tactical opportunity was missed: a knight fork on f3 would have won the queen, but the opponent's move order avoided it. Recognizing such tactics is crucial, but also note that the opponent's move was fortunate because it allowed them to survive.
notes.teaches: Always look for tactical motifs like forks, pins, and skewers. When you spot a tactic, verify that the opponent cannot escape with a counter-tactic or a resourceful move.
notes.plans: Continue to look for tactical shots, but also be prepared to handle the opponent's defensive resources.

notes.explains: The defender notes that pieces on dark squares can be a target, and sacrifices might be possible. However, with two rooks versus a queen, the defender acknowledges that coordination is key and that the opponent's accurate play makes simple tactics unlikely.
notes.teaches: Always be alert to tactical possibilities, but also recognize the resilience of certain material balances; coordination is essential.
notes.plans: Look for sacrifices or tactical shots, but prioritize coordination and solid defense.

notes.explains: After White recaptures on e5, Black's queen moves are aimless, and Black fails to notice that the knight on c7 is hanging. White also misses the fork Nxc7+, which would win material.
notes.teaches: Always look for tactical opportunities, especially when your opponent's pieces are undefended or loose. A simple fork can win material if you take the time to calculate.
notes.plans: White should play Nxc7+ forking the king and rook, winning the exchange.

notes.explains: When the opponent has violated opening principles, tactical opportunities often arise. Here, a pin (or x-ray) along a line with the rook and king can win the queen because the queen is overloaded defending against mate.
notes.teaches: After the opponent breaks principles, look for concrete tactics like pins, forks, and discovered attacks. A pin against the king can be decisive.
notes.plans: Identify the tactical motif (pin, fork, etc.) and execute it, but also be alert to repeated tactical ideas in the same position.

notes.explains: In a sharp position, a move like e4 can be risky but can also create immediate threats. Preparing it with a knight move first is more accurate, but sometimes you can save a position out of nowhere with a tactical blow.
notes.teaches: When a queen appears on a key square, visualize or physically draw the lines it controls. This helps you spot mating nets and tactical opportunities.
notes.plans: If the queen lands on a square like b7, it can be checkmate. Always check the queen's lines before committing.

notes.explains: White has a winning position, but then plays a check that is a blunder because it allows Black to capture a piece. Even in a winning position, you must stay alert and not give the opponent counterplay. The check was tempting, but it hung a piece.
notes.teaches: Never assume the game is over just because you are winning. Always check for tactics and avoid giving the opponent chances to get back into the game. Prefer moves that maintain your advantage without unnecessary risks.
notes.plans: After the blunder, White is still better but must consolidate and avoid further mistakes. Look for moves that defend the hanging pieces and keep the attack going.

notes.explains: White misses the mate and plays knight e6, allowing the evaluation to drop. Later, white again misses a mate and instead plays a move that hangs a rook, but black fails to capitalize fully, and the game remains unclear.
notes.teaches: In sharp positions, missing a tactical opportunity can swing the game. Always be alert for checks, captures, and threats, especially when the opponent's king is exposed.
notes.plans: After missing a tactic, regroup and look for the next best move. Even if you miss a mate, you can still fight for equality or advantage if you stay accurate.

notes.explains: A knight move to c7 is a mistake because it allows a fork. The better move was to check on e8 and then push the pawn, but that would allow the king to run up and take it, so the clump of pieces on that side is a concern.
notes.teaches: Always be alert to tactical motifs like forks. When your pieces are clustered, they are vulnerable to such tactics.
notes.plans: Black should avoid the fork and instead reposition the knight to a better square like d5.

notes.explains: The position is highly tactical, with the queen overloaded defending both a bishop and a pawn. A knight move to b5 creates multiple threats: a fork, a pawn capture, and a potential knight fork on c7. This level of calculation is characteristic of strong play.
notes.teaches: In tactical positions, look for moves that create multiple threats simultaneously, especially when the opponent's pieces are overloaded. Calculate deeply to ensure the tactics work in your favor.
notes.plans: Consider moves like knight to d6, which attacks both a bishop and a knight, and if captured, leaves you two pawns up. Be ready to sacrifice material if it leads to a decisive advantage.

notes.explains: Black's rook to e8 allows white to play g5, attacking the bishop. The computer suggests b4, which destabilizes the position but is considered reasonable. White chooses g5, winning a pawn after bishop f5.
notes.teaches: When your opponent's move creates a tactical opportunity, consider both aggressive pawn pushes and quieter moves that maintain tension. Sometimes the computer's 'ugly' moves are viable.
notes.plans: After winning the pawn, consolidate and maintain the extra material while keeping the king safe.

notes.explains: The game becomes chaotic with the opponent playing very accurately and quickly. The speaker feels spooked and struggles to find counterplay, even considering moves like Rc8 and Rc5, but they are not viable. Eventually, the opponent blunders a fork.
notes.teaches: In sharp positions, stay calm and look for tactical opportunities even when the opponent seems to be playing well. Sometimes the opponent will make a mistake under pressure; be ready to exploit it.
notes.plans: Keep the position tense and wait for the opponent to err. If a fork is available, take it, but also be mindful of your own king's safety and avoid creating weaknesses.

notes.explains: After the inaccuracy, the player allowed the opponent to create a winning position. The opponent then blundered a fork, but later resigned in a position where they were actually winning (rook c8 check, take take take).
notes.teaches: Always check for tactical resources before resigning; even in a winning position, a single blunder can turn the tables. Conversely, when you have a winning position, stay alert to avoid blunders.
notes.plans: In a winning position, look for the most forcing and safe continuations to convert, such as checks and captures that simplify.

notes.explains: After playing principled chess, the position becomes resilient and full of threats. Here, the player has multiple threats: recapturing a pawn, a knight fork on c2, and other tactical ideas.
notes.teaches: When you follow sound opening principles, your position will naturally contain tactical resources. Look for ways to create multiple threats that the opponent cannot all parry.
notes.plans: Identify the immediate threats and choose the most forcing continuation, such as a fork or a check, to win material.

notes.explains: After the opponent's mistake, the player autopiloted and recaptured a pawn on c3, missing a stronger move on e7 that would have attacked multiple pieces and won material.
notes.teaches: Always look for forcing moves that create multiple threats. Before recapturing, consider if there is a more active move that wins material or gains a decisive advantage.
notes.plans: If the stronger move had been played, the opponent would lose material regardless of how they recaptured, so the plan is to calculate such tactical sequences fully.

notes.explains: White is winning because of a lead in development and a safer king. However, White makes a mistake with Queen h6, allowing Black's Queen c5 check to win the bishop. The computer suggests Bishop f5, which is even stronger, threatening mate and keeping the attack.
notes.teaches: When you have a winning advantage, avoid moves that hang pieces or allow counterplay. Always consider the opponent's checks and captures. Sometimes a more forcing move is better than a natural one.
notes.plans: White should look for ways to maintain the attack while safeguarding the king and pieces. Black should exploit any inaccuracies to regain material and counterattack.

notes.explains: When your opponent has a hanging piece or a fork, you must be alert. Even at lower levels, players will spot simple tactics like forks, so you need to have a response ready.
notes.teaches: Be careful about placing pieces on squares where they can be forked. Always check for tactical threats before committing a piece.
notes.plans: If your piece is attacked, find a move that both saves it and maintains your advantage, such as moving the queen to e7.

notes.explains: The position has many tactical possibilities, including back-rank threats, pins, and forks. The opponent must be careful not to leave pieces loose, as 'loose pieces drop off'.
notes.teaches: Always be aware of loose pieces and tactical motifs like pins, forks, and back-rank mates. Use these to create threats and win material.
notes.plans: Look for moves that create multiple threats, such as rook moves that attack pawns or set up forks with the queen.

notes.explains: The move e4 attacks the knight and creates a pin, leading to a winning tactic. The opponent's only move is to retreat the knight, but after the exchange, the pawn advances to d3, winning material.
notes.teaches: When a pawn advances to the sixth rank, it can be a powerful asset, but sometimes it can become a liability if it gets blockaded. Calculate carefully whether the deep pawn is good or bad.
notes.plans: After winning the pawn, consolidate by developing pieces and maintaining the extra material, while being aware of the opponent's counterplay.

notes.explains: With the rook and queen opposite each other on the same file, there is always the possibility of a tactical strike. The opponent's move allowed a pawn push that dropped the evaluation bar, indicating a winning advantage.
notes.teaches: Recognize when enemy pieces are aligned on a file or diagonal, as that often creates tactical opportunities. Intuition for such patterns develops with experience, but you can train it by studying typical motifs.
notes.plans: Calculate the forcing lines to ensure the advantage is real and not just a temporary tactic.

notes.explains: The attacker missed a brilliant resource: a knight move that creates two unavoidable mating threats. The opponent's only defenses are insufficient, and the attack is winning.
notes.teaches: Always look for quiet moves that create multiple threats. A single piece can often deliver a decisive blow if it attacks the king from a strong outpost. Calculate all forcing moves, including quiet ones, before committing to a plan.
notes.plans: Execute the winning move and convert the attack.

notes.explains: The opponent played f3, a pawn move that fails to address the pin and allows a tactical blow. This is a common mistake at lower levels: moving a pawn when the position requires dealing with a pin or a threat.
notes.teaches: Pawn moves that don't address the opponent's threats can be punished. When your pawn is pinned to the king, moving it can be illegal or disastrous. Always check if your intended move allows a tactic.
notes.plans: Black exploits the mistake by capturing on g2 with the queen, winning material and exposing the king.

notes.explains: When the opponent attacks the queen with a pawn, they often assume the queen must retreat, but if the queen can capture a pawn and give check or create a bigger threat, the attack backfires. Here, the bishop was pinned, so the queen trade was not an option for the opponent, and the pawn push opened the king.
notes.teaches: Before making a move that attacks a piece, always check where that piece can go and whether it can create a counter-threat. A piece that is pinned or defended may be able to strike back.
notes.plans: If the opponent makes such a mistake, take the pawn and follow up by exploiting the open king and the pinned pieces.

notes.explains: In a sharp position, the opponent may have a defensive resource like queen to c6, which seems to hold but actually loses immediately. The key is to spot tactical motifs like a discovered attack on the queen.
notes.teaches: Always apply CCA (Checks, Captures, Attacks) to find forcing moves. Even when a move seems natural, look for tactical refutations that exploit the opponent's king safety.
notes.plans: If the opponent plays queen to c6, respond with rook takes c6, winning the queen due to the pin on the rook.

notes.explains: The move knight a5 is a strong resource because it attacks the queen while also trapping it, as the queen has to protect a key pawn and has no safe squares.
notes.teaches: Look for moves that combine attack with restriction, especially when the opponent's queen becomes overloaded.
notes.plans: If the knight a5 is played, the queen is stuck, and black can follow up with queen a2 to win material.

notes.explains: A tactical idea like rook takes d5 may look tempting, but it fails because the defender has multiple ways to meet it: moving the queen to guard, capturing the knight, or even ignoring the sacrifice to take on b2.
notes.teaches: Before sacrificing, check if the opponent has simple defensive resources. If they can ignore the sacrifice and win material, it's not a real threat.
notes.plans: Keep the material advantage and continue improving pieces rather than forcing tactics.

notes.explains: A move like rook takes bishop, followed by rook takes knight, trades two minor pieces for a rook, which is generally good. But if the opponent can simply retreat, the attack was a waste of time.
notes.teaches: Think in sequences of two moves; evaluate whether a tactical operation has a concrete follow-up before starting it.
notes.plans: Look for a knight fork that wins material, but be wary of the opponent's counterattacks.

notes.explains: When you have many pawns on dark squares, your dark-squared bishop is often blocked by your own pawns and has limited scope, while the light-squared bishop may have more activity.
notes.teaches: Consider trading a bishop that is constrained by your own pawn structure, especially if it is a bad bishop.

notes.explains: To evaluate bishops, count pawns on the board. If the pawns are balanced (e.g., 4 vs 4), the bishops are roughly equal. But the next step is to see if the bishop has mobility; if it's blocked by its own pawns, it's a bad bishop.
notes.teaches: A bishop's value depends on its activity, not just the pawn count. Look for whether the bishop is blocked by pawns on its own color; if so, it's a problem piece.
notes.plans: If your opponent has a bad bishop, try to keep it blocked and target it. If you have a bad bishop, seek to trade it or free it by moving pawns.

notes.explains: Black traded their dark-squared bishop for a knight, but this is a positional mistake because Black has many pawns on light squares. The light-squared bishop will be severely restricted, and the dark-squared bishop was essential for defending the weakened dark squares.
notes.teaches: When your pawns are fixed on one color, keep the bishop that controls the opposite color. Trading it can leave you with a 'bad' bishop and weaknesses.

notes.explains: When a player has many pawns on light squares, their light-squared bishop is often a 'bad bishop' because it's blocked by its own pawns. In such positions, the dark-squared bishop becomes crucial for defending the weak light squares and should not be traded off.
notes.teaches: Avoid trading your bishop that is the only defender of the color complex where your pawns are fixed. Keep it to protect the weaknesses created by your pawn structure.
notes.plans: If you have a bad bishop, try to improve it or trade it for the opponent's good bishop, but never give up the bishop that covers the squares your pawns cannot.

notes.explains: Even when down material, if your pieces are poorly developed and your king is unsafe, the opponent can be better. Here, despite being up pawns, black's pieces are not active and the king is vulnerable.
notes.teaches: Development and king safety often outweigh material advantages, especially in the opening and early middlegame.

notes.explains: Black has not developed several pieces by move 17, which is a serious issue. The opponent's light-squared bishop moved once and was then captured, showing a lack of development.
notes.teaches: Development is crucial. If your opponent lags in development, you should open the position to exploit their king's vulnerability and piece inactivity.
notes.plans: Use your lead in development to create threats, open lines, and attack the opponent's king before they can catch up.

notes.explains: When the opponent launches an early attack, sticking to sound principles like castling and developing can neutralize it. Even if you lose a pawn, following good principles often leads to compensation in activity or king safety.
notes.teaches: Don't panic when facing aggressive moves; trust your development and look for ways to complete your own setup. Sometimes losing a pawn is acceptable if you get a lead in development or the opponent's king remains exposed.
notes.plans: Castle, complete development, and then exploit the opponent's overextension.

notes.explains: White has a significant advantage due to the bishop pair and black's underdevelopment. Black needs several moves to catch up, allowing white to build pressure.
notes.teaches: In the opening, a lead in development and the bishop pair can be decisive. Punish slow moves by opening the center and activating your pieces.
notes.plans: Short castle and then break in the center with trades, using the bishops to dominate the queenside and the rook to control open files.

notes.explains: White's move c4 is confusing because it doesn't develop a piece or address the immediate threats. In a position where you're behind in development, you need to get your pieces out, not make pawn moves that don't contribute.
notes.teaches: In the opening and early middlegame, prioritize development. Moves that don't develop or create threats often waste time and allow your opponent to strengthen their position.
notes.plans: White should aim to develop the knights and bishops and connect the rooks, while black should continue to press the advantage.

notes.explains: White repeatedly fails to develop their queenside pieces (knight, bishop, rook) and loses material due to hanging pieces. Black's rook is active and gobbling pawns.
notes.teaches: Neglecting development leaves pieces vulnerable and allows the opponent to win material for free. Always bring your pieces into play before starting attacks.
notes.plans: Develop the knight to c3 and bishop to e3, and connect rooks to defend the back rank.

notes.explains: White is down material but has a significant development advantage: Black's pieces are still stuck on the back rank. White can use this lead in development to create threats and overwhelm Black before they can untangle.
notes.teaches: When behind in material, compensate with activity and development. Centralize your rooks and bring all pieces into the game to create pressure against an opponent whose pieces are passive.
notes.plans: White should continue developing, centralizing rooks, and preparing to attack the black king, which remains in the center.

notes.explains: When the opponent's king remains in the center, piece activity becomes paramount. Developing all pieces to the middle immediately creates threats, such as a knight jumping to c4 to hit the queen and then to d6, which is devastating because the rook defends it and the king is exposed.
notes.teaches: Rapid development to the center is key when the opponent's king is uncastled. Look for tactical jumps that exploit the king's exposure, like a knight fork on d6.
notes.plans: Continue building pressure, aiming for a knight on c4 and then d6, or other central breakthroughs, to exploit the opponent's uncastled king.

notes.explains: Black finally activates the bishop with bishop b7, but it's too late; white is winning. The speaker points out that if black had played g6 earlier, the bishop could have been activated with tempo.
notes.teaches: Develop your pieces early, especially bishops. A bishop stuck on its original square is a liability. Look for moves that develop with tempo (attacking something).

notes.explains: When the opponent makes a move with no threat, you should use the time to develop your pieces. Here, the knight was brought into the game and rooks connected.
notes.teaches: If your opponent's move doesn't threaten anything, prioritize development and improving your pieces.
notes.plans: Complete development, connect rooks, and then look for active plans.

notes.explains: In the game, the opponent's slightly bad development allowed the doubling of their pawns and left their bishop misplaced. Even when material was equal or slightly worse, the positional weaknesses gave lasting pressure.
notes.teaches: Small development inaccuracies can lead to long-term weaknesses like doubled pawns or a bad bishop. Prefer moves that develop pieces to active squares and avoid creating permanent weaknesses.
notes.plans: Keep pressuring the weak points, and if the opponent defends well, be patient and improve your pieces.

notes.explains: In the position after the opening, White has a hanging bishop and Black has a comfortable position. Black develops with tempo, attacking the knight, and White spends a long time thinking, which is a time management issue.
notes.teaches: Developing moves that attack pieces are often good because they force the opponent to respond and can save time. Also, avoid spending too much time on simple moves; manage your clock.
notes.plans: Continue developing, castle, and look for opportunities to win the hanging bishop or create threats.

notes.explains: In the resulting Caro-Kann structure, Black should avoid rushing with moves like ...d4 that attack the queen but don't develop; instead, developing a bishop to b4 or e7 is better.
notes.teaches: Don't play 'feel-good' moves that give the opponent a chance to improve their pieces; prioritize development and long-term pressure over immediate threats.
notes.plans: Develop the remaining pieces, castle, and then use the pawn structure to restrict White's play while preparing a kingside attack if White overextends.

notes.explains: White plays Be2, a passive move that doesn't address the threats. Better moves like Bd3, Bc4, or Bb5 would develop actively and put pressure on Black. Be2 only prepares castling, but it allows Black to capture the e4-pawn with Qxe4.
notes.teaches: In the opening and middlegame, develop pieces to active squares where they exert influence. Passive moves that only prepare castling can be too slow if they allow your opponent to seize the initiative.
notes.plans: White should develop the bishop actively, e.g., Bc4, to maintain pressure and prepare castling.

notes.explains: The rooks are still undeveloped, and the knight needs repositioning. Playing Rc8 is a natural move to activate the last piece and prepare to attack the pawn.
notes.teaches: Develop your rooks to open files and centralize them; reroute pieces to better squares even if it takes time.
notes.plans: Bring the rooks to the center, reposition the knight, and use the pawn break to open the position.

notes.explains: A position where you have nothing developed and are far from castling is critical. The opponent can launch an attack with pieces like bishop c4 and rook to the open file, threatening mate.
notes.teaches: In the opening, losing even a little time can lead to a losing attack. Always prioritize development and castling to avoid such disasters.
notes.plans: If you are in this situation, try to trade pieces, block threats, and find a way to develop and castle, but recognize that the position may already be lost.

notes.explains: Black's move f5 opens the position, but Black is severely behind in development, so opening lines only benefits White's better-developed pieces.
notes.teaches: Do not open the position when you are behind in development; open lines give the opponent's active pieces more targets.
notes.plans: Black should avoid pawn breaks that open the position and instead focus on completing development, while White should exploit the open lines to attack.

notes.explains: The speaker considers bringing the second knight into the game, noting that even if it's not the absolute best, there are many good moves and no blunders.
notes.teaches: In winning positions, prioritize development and activity over finding the single best move. Use your pieces; don't leave them idle.
notes.plans: Bring all pieces into play, then double rooks on open files.

notes.explains: Black has no advantage after 12 moves; White has played reasonably. Black should not rush but continue developing, bringing rooks to the center to defend and participate.
notes.teaches: In equal positions, prioritize completing development and centralizing rooks. Avoid forcing moves that don't improve your position.
notes.plans: Finish development, bring rooks to central files, and wait for the opponent to make a mistake.

notes.explains: Moves like Bg4 or Ng4 can trap the queen or win material because the opponent's pieces are not fully developed. The queen should not lead the attack alone; it needs support.
notes.teaches: Before launching an attack, ensure your pieces are developed. Use tactical motifs like pins and forks to exploit the opponent's lack of coordination.
notes.plans: Look for ways to win the bishop or knight, and then convert the material advantage.

notes.explains: After winning a pawn, the game is not over; you still need to play solidly. Developing the bishop to a long diagonal is strong, but you must be alert to tactics like knight forks on e5, so queen to d3 is a safe way to avoid issues.
notes.teaches: Even with an advantage, keep developing and avoid tactical pitfalls. Place pieces on active squares, like a bishop on a long diagonal.
notes.plans: Castle, develop the bishop, and consider queen moves that avoid tactical tricks.

notes.explains: After the opening, the speaker considers various moves like bishop b7 and castling, and notes that a lazy retreat could allow g4 and f4, creating kingside pressure.
notes.teaches: Avoid passive moves that give the opponent free pawn breaks; instead, maintain flexibility and counterplay.
notes.plans: Develop harmoniously, castle, and prepare to support the center with moves like queen to reinforce the pawn.

notes.explains: Castling long can be a good way to activate the rook and bring it into the attack, especially when the center is open and the king can find safety on the other side.
notes.teaches: Consider long castling when it helps develop the rook and the king is safer on that side.

notes.explains: Black plays ...Qe7+, forcing the king to move, and then ...Rh7, defending the f7 knight. White retreats the knight to g5, attacking the rook again. Now White plays d5, but this is not the best. Castling is better, and long castling is preferable because it brings the rook to the d-file, supporting the pawn push.
notes.teaches: When your king is still in the center and the position is opening up, castling is often a priority. Long castling can be better if it places a rook on a useful file and keeps the king safe.
notes.plans: White should castle long, then use the rook on d1 to support a central pawn break, while keeping the attack on the kingside.

notes.explains: When your opponent is checking you repeatedly, you should not just give checks without a plan; eventually the checks run out and you may lose material or the initiative.
notes.teaches: Perpetual checks are only useful if they lead to a draw or a concrete gain; otherwise, they can be a waste of time and allow the opponent to consolidate.

notes.explains: In a winning position, it's important to keep pressing and look for the most forcing continuation, such as checks and captures, to convert the advantage.
notes.teaches: When you have a large advantage, look for forcing moves that increase the pressure and lead to mate or material gain.

notes.explains: After White's poor opening, Black has a winning position. The engine suggests moves like ...e4 to trap the queen, but even simple developing moves maintain the advantage.
notes.teaches: When you have a large advantage, you don't need to find the flashiest move; just keep developing and avoid hanging pieces. Solid play converts the advantage.
notes.plans: Finish development, castle, and then target White's weaknesses.

notes.explains: With a decisive material advantage, White can afford to make moves that would normally be risky, such as leaving the king in the center or sacrificing pawns. The opponent's counterplay is easily neutralized.
notes.teaches: When converting a winning position, prioritize activity and threats over safety. Use your extra material to fuel an attack, and don't be afraid to give back some material to keep the initiative.
notes.plans: Open the king's position with pawn breaks like g6, and look for mating patterns or ways to win more material. Keep the queen active and avoid unnecessary complications.

notes.explains: The game was won using only the queen and the g-pawn, without the bishop and rook. The positional advantage from the opening made the win possible even with limited pieces.
notes.teaches: A superior position can convert with minimal material; the key is to keep the initiative and not allow counterplay. If the opponent tries to create counterplay, trading queens simplifies to a winning endgame.
notes.plans: If the opponent plays queen f6, either continue the attack with bishop d2 or simply trade queens to eliminate all counterplay.

notes.explains: In a winning position, it is easy to go wrong. Here, White misses several forced mates and instead plays moves that allow Black back into the game.
notes.teaches: When you have a decisive advantage, take your time to find the most forcing continuation; do not rush and allow counterplay.
notes.plans: Look for checks, captures, and threats that limit the opponent's options.

notes.explains: The attacker is up two pieces (five points of material) but the position has become complicated. The opponent is generating counterplay, and the attacker must be careful not to allow the position to become unclear.
notes.teaches: The easiest way to convert a winning position is to prioritize king safety. Do not allow unnecessary complications that give the opponent counterplay.
notes.plans: Consolidate by castling or moving the queen to safety, ensuring the king is secure before continuing the attack.

notes.explains: When the opponent has lost their queen, the game is effectively won, but you must still be careful about tactical threats like back-rank mates or time pressure. The position is winning, so the focus is on converting cleanly.
notes.teaches: After a material advantage, the main dangers are tactical oversights, so continue to play accurately. Think before making mistakes, not after.
notes.plans: Convert the material advantage by simplifying, avoiding counterplay, and ensuring king safety.

notes.explains: When you are up material but your king is exposed, you must prioritize safety and conversion over further heroics. Here, the king can hide on f1 and block checks, allowing long castling.
notes.teaches: In a winning position, neutralize counterplay by securing your king and forcing trades, even if it means giving back some material.
notes.plans: Long castle, then trade queens or rooks to reach a technically winning endgame.

notes.explains: With a huge material advantage, the priority is to avoid blunders and continue taking free material, but also to consider the most active continuation, such as applying pressure with pieces rather than just capturing.
notes.teaches: When winning, keep your pieces coordinated and avoid unnecessary risks; look for ways to increase pressure or force mate rather than just grabbing material.
notes.plans: Take the free knight, then continue to attack the opponent's pieces, possibly using checks or threats to win more material or force a decisive advantage.

notes.explains: The opponent is down a queen, and despite playing quickly, the material deficit is decisive. The focus should be on safe development and converting the advantage.
notes.teaches: When you are up material, prioritize safety and simplification. Avoid unnecessary risks and bring pieces to active squares while maintaining the advantage.
notes.plans: Bring the queen to safety, develop the rook, and address potential back-rank weaknesses before proceeding with the attack.

notes.explains: White has won a queen for a piece, but the game continues. White must convert the material advantage by developing pieces and coordinating an attack.
notes.teaches: After winning material, focus on activating all your pieces and creating threats. Do not become complacent; keep the pressure on.
notes.plans: Develop the rook to an open file, bring the queen and other pieces to bear on the enemy king, and force exchanges that simplify to a winning endgame if necessary.

notes.explains: The player considered a move that would pry apart the opponent's defenses, but chose a more solid development first. Later, they saw a winning tactic involving a rook move that forced the opponent to respond, leading to a mating attack.
notes.teaches: Sometimes it is better to improve your pieces first before executing a tactical blow. When you have a winning position, look for the most forcing continuation that leaves the opponent no good options.
notes.plans: In a winning position, aim to convert by forcing trades or creating threats that the opponent cannot meet. Use checks and captures to drive the king into a mating net.

notes.explains: In a winning position, there are two main ways to convert: trade all the pieces into a simple endgame, or coordinate your pieces to launch a mating attack. Here, the queen and knight work together to create threats that force the opponent's pawns forward, exposing the king.
notes.teaches: When you have a material or positional advantage, choose a clear conversion method: either simplify by trading pieces or build a coordinated attack. Do not drift without a plan.
notes.plans: If attacking, keep the queen and knight coordinated, aiming at the king and forcing pawn moves that weaken the enemy king's shelter.

notes.explains: After trading off the knight, the position becomes winning. The opponent's pawns are weak, and black has a material advantage. The key is to blockade the queen and bishop from having vision, then use the open file to invade.
notes.teaches: When converting a material advantage, prevent counterplay by blockading enemy pieces. Use open files to penetrate and win more pawns.
notes.plans: Block the queen's and bishop's lines, then double rooks on the open file to target the weak pawn.

notes.explains: After the opponent's mistake, we have a winning position. The plan involves a backward knight move to f5, which targets the queen and defends against mate, creating a fork.
notes.teaches: In winning positions, look for tactical resources that both defend and attack. Converting a winning position requires precise, forcing moves.
notes.plans: Use the knight to create threats and force the opponent into a cramped position. If they blunder, take advantage immediately.

notes.explains: Even with a dominant position, accuracy is required to convert. The opponent nearly equalized because of imprecise play. A move like Knight B5 would have been completely winning, but a prophylactic move allowed counterplay.
notes.teaches: When you have a large advantage, look for the most forcing and clinical continuation. Prophylactic moves can be good, but sometimes direct attacks are better. Always calculate the most precise moves to maintain the advantage.
notes.plans: In similar positions, seek the most direct winning plan, such as a knight fork or a decisive attack, rather than allowing the opponent to regroup.

notes.explains: Even when the opponent is clearly lost, they may keep playing, hoping for a mistake. It's important to stay focused and finish the game efficiently.
notes.teaches: Never assume the game is over until it is; keep playing accurately and look for the quickest way to win.

notes.explains: Even when hopelessly down on material, if the opponent cannot deliver mate, the game is not over. The defender can keep playing and hope for a mistake.
notes.teaches: Never resign while there is still a chance, however small, that the opponent will blunder or fail to find the win.
notes.plans: Keep making legal moves, avoid immediate mate, and put pressure on the opponent to convert.

notes.explains: When the opponent has a huge material advantage but cannot find mate, they often repeat checks or shuffle pieces. The defender can exploit this by staying alert for a chance to escape or even turn the tables.
notes.teaches: In a lost position, look for ways to force the opponent to show their plan; they may not know how to convert and may repeat moves or miss simple tactics.
notes.plans: Keep the king safe, avoid unnecessary pawn moves that open lines, and wait for the opponent to make a mistake.

notes.explains: When facing a pawn storm on the flank, it is often better to move the attacked knight rather than push pawns in front of it. Moving the knight to d7 allows a later h5 to lock the position and reduce the attacker's space.
notes.teaches: When defending against a flank attack, avoid pushing pawns that weaken your own position. Instead, reposition pieces to allow pawn moves that close the position and limit the attacker's options.
notes.plans: After moving the knight to d7, if the opponent plays g5, respond with h5 to lock the kingside and prevent further pawn advances.

notes.explains: When under attack, pushing the pawn that is being attacked by an enemy pawn can create weaknesses and is generally undesirable. Instead, moving the knight to d7 prepares h5 to lock the pawn structure, which helps defend.
notes.teaches: In defense, avoid pushing pawns that are under attack; instead, reposition pieces to support a pawn lock that limits the opponent's attacking chances.
notes.plans: After ...Nd7, if White plays g5, respond with ...h5 to fix the pawns and reduce the opponent's attacking potential.

notes.explains: When defending against a flank attack, the defender should avoid opening lines unnecessarily. Taking once and pushing the second pawn is a common rule to keep the position closed.
notes.teaches: To blunt an attack, don't capture every pawn that comes at you. Sometimes just pushing your own pawn (like a3) stops the attack without opening lines for the opponent.
notes.plans: If the opponent attacks on the flank, consider a quiet pawn push to calm the attack rather than trading, which would open the position.

notes.explains: When your knight is attacked and you need to defend it, the cleanest way is often to use checks, captures, or attacks to create a counter-threat that forces the opponent to react, giving you time to save the knight.
notes.teaches: In defensive positions, look for tactical resources like checks that can change the evaluation. A check can force the opponent to respond, allowing you to move your threatened piece to safety.
notes.plans: If you have a check that forces the queen to capture, you can then recapture and your knight escapes. This is a common defensive motif.

notes.explains: When the opponent is attacking, it's easy to focus only on defense and miss that a piece left a square undefended. Here, a rook move to d8 would have allowed the queen to be captured because the queen no longer defended the pawn.
notes.teaches: Before moving a piece, check what it was defending. A retreating move can create new weaknesses. Always consider the opponent's threats as well as your own.
notes.plans: Exploit the opponent's defensive mistakes by capturing undefended pawns and forcing favorable trades.

notes.explains: When facing a Greek gift, the best defense is often to move forward rather than backward, as retreating allows the queen to rush in.
notes.teaches: In king attacks, advancing the king can sometimes be safer than retreating, but each position must be evaluated concretely.
notes.plans: If defending, consider forward king moves to escape the attack.

notes.explains: In a bad position with a weak king, you must find ways to counterattack or create complications. Here, the opponent has a strong initiative, and you need to be resourceful in defense.
notes.teaches: When on the defensive, look for active moves that create threats or force the opponent to react, rather than passively retreating.
notes.plans: Identify checks, captures, and threats that can disrupt the opponent's plans and give you breathing room.

notes.explains: When facing pressure, a key defensive resource is to trade off the opponent's active pieces. Playing Bb5 in a position where the opponent's bishop is causing pressure helps simplify and bring more of your own pieces into play.
notes.teaches: In difficult positions, look for trades that remove the opponent's most active pieces, even if the move looks passive. This can relieve pressure and activate your own pieces.
notes.plans: Continue to trade pieces that are pressuring your position, and bring your rooks into play to defend and counterattack.

notes.explains: When facing a sacrifice, the defender must be precise: moving the king is often best, and you must find a safe square for the bishop to avoid tactics.
notes.teaches: In defense, prioritize king safety and piece coordination; look for moves that neutralize the attacker's initiative, like trading the key attacking piece.
notes.plans: Move the king, place the bishop on a safe square like b4 to trade, and get the rook into play.

notes.explains: The opponent finds a series of strong defensive moves, including queen checks and a knight maneuver, which disrupts the plan. The position becomes complicated, and the player must back up the rook to avoid threats like Nf4.
notes.teaches: In sharp positions, the opponent may find resourceful defenses. Stay flexible and be ready to adjust plans, even if it means retreating a piece to maintain safety.
notes.plans: Continue developing, keep the king safe, and look for ways to exploit the opponent's weaknesses without overextending.

notes.explains: The attacker is worried about specific defensive resources, such as a knight moving to a key defensive square that doesn't cover the mating square but covers the attacking piece. This defensive idea is hard to see and can refute a natural attacking move.
notes.teaches: When calculating an attack, consider not only direct blocks and captures but also defensive moves that indirectly defend by covering the attacker or creating counterplay. These 'quiet' defensive moves are often the hardest to foresee.
notes.plans: After the opponent's best defensive move, reassess the attack and look for alternative ways to continue, possibly by switching the point of attack.

notes.explains: We are under pressure, with our king potentially exposed. The opponent has a bishop on e5 and a knight that could infiltrate. We consider retreating with knight d7, but that feels dangerous because it allows the opponent to keep attacking. Instead, we look to trade pieces to alleviate the pressure.
notes.teaches: When your king is under attack, trading pieces can be a key defensive resource. It reduces the attacker's forces and can relieve the pressure, even if it means giving up some activity.
notes.plans: Trade pieces, especially the dark-squared bishop, by playing knight c5 or other trades, and try to kick out the opponent's knight to reduce the attack.

notes.explains: The opponent plays bishop f6, and we notice that bishop takes a7 is a possible move for them, but it looks bad. We consider taking with the queen to avoid checkmate threats. The opponent plays queen g3, keeping the queen on the board, but we see that b2 is available to take.
notes.teaches: When defending against a king attack, it's crucial to consider captures that remove the opponent's attacking pieces. Taking with the queen can be a strong defensive move because the queen is a powerful defender and can also counterattack.
notes.plans: Take on b2 with the knight or queen, and continue trading pieces to simplify the position and reduce the attack.

notes.explains: We have successfully traded pieces and the position has simplified. The opponent has two attacking pieces, but they can't get a third one to work. We have a strong defender in the queen. The opponent's bishop and queen form a battery, but it's not threatening. We consider trading knights to remove the piece covering our king's escape square.
notes.teaches: In defense, it's important to identify the key attacking piece and trade it off. Removing the piece that covers your king's escape square can be a clever defensive resource, as it gives your king more room and reduces the attack.
notes.plans: Trade knights to remove the attacking piece, then continue simplifying and use the queen to defend against any remaining threats.

notes.explains: In a rook and pawn endgame, the side with the extra pawns must be careful: if the opponent can sacrifice a piece for the last pawn, the game may be drawn. Here, the defender's king is active and the pawns are blocked, making the win tricky.
notes.teaches: In pawn endgames, an active king is crucial. The side with material advantage must avoid allowing the opponent to trade off the last pawn or force a fortress.
notes.plans: The winning side should use the king to support the pawns, while the defending side should try to blockade and create counterplay.

notes.explains: With queens off the board, the game simplifies, but the side with a material deficit can still fight for a draw if the opponent's king is exposed or if there are perpetual check possibilities. The position is still winning for the stronger side, but only with accurate play.
notes.teaches: In queenless middlegames and endgames, king safety and activity become paramount. A material advantage is not enough if the opponent can generate threats against your king.
notes.plans: When you are up material, trade pieces to reduce counterplay, but keep your king safe. When you are down, activate your pieces and look for perpetual check or stalemate tricks.

notes.explains: In a complex endgame with unequal material, the engine may prefer a line that wins a bishop and reaches a favorable pawn endgame, but human play can be more difficult. The key is to keep the initiative and avoid unnecessary complications.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, simplify to a known winning endgame if possible. Avoid unclear complications that give the opponent chances.
notes.plans: Trade pieces to reach a simple winning pawn endgame, or use your extra material to create passed pawns.

notes.explains: In a queen versus rook and pawn endgame, the side with the queen often has winning chances, but the defender can create counterplay by activating the rook and linking rooks on the enemy's second rank, as black did here.
notes.teaches: In endgames, active piece play is crucial. Even when behind in material, look for ways to create threats and coordinate your pieces to maximize their activity.
notes.plans: For the side with the queen, use checks and threats to force the enemy king into a vulnerable position, then win the rook or deliver mate. For the defender, keep the rook active and look for perpetual check or stalemate ideas.

notes.explains: With a rook and bishop against a rook, you are winning. You should bring your king forward and continue taking free pawns.
notes.teaches: In a winning endgame, activate your king and capture free material while avoiding unnecessary risks.
notes.plans: Advance the king, take any free pawns, and simplify further to convert the advantage.

notes.explains: In a rook and pawn endgame, the main goal is to promote a pawn. Winning more pawns increases your chances, and keeping pieces protected is still important.
notes.teaches: In endgames with rooks and pawns, prioritize pushing passed pawns and using rooks to support them. Rooks work well together on the same rank or file, and a rook can cut off the enemy king.
notes.plans: Push your pawns together, use your rook to cut off the enemy king, and aim to promote. If you have a material advantage, trading pieces is often good.

notes.explains: When you are up material and the opponent has only a rook, you can often hide your king in the corner or even walk it across the board because one rook alone cannot deliver checkmate.
notes.teaches: In king and rook vs. king and pawns endgames, the king can often be used actively because the opponent's rook cannot mate without support. Use your king to help promote pawns.
notes.plans: Trade off pieces to simplify, then use your extra material to promote a pawn. If low on time, win all pawns to avoid losing on time, but remember the insufficient material rule.

notes.explains: In a rook versus knight endgame with extra pawns, the winning plan is to push the pawns and create a passed pawn. The knight can only give checks, but the king can stay safe and the rook can support the pawn's promotion.
notes.teaches: In rook vs knight endgames, don't chase the knight. Push your passed pawns. Use the rook to cut off the enemy king and support the pawn. Aim for a ladder mate or promote to a second rook.
notes.plans: Push the pawns, keep the king safe, and use the rook to control key ranks. When the pawn reaches the seventh rank, use the rook to deliver mate or promote.

notes.explains: In the endgame, having an extra pawn and a safer king is a significant advantage. The plan is to improve piece activity, create threats, and avoid unnecessary queen trades when you are ahead in material.
notes.teaches: When you are up material, avoid trading queens if it reduces your winning chances. Instead, use your pieces to create threats and increase the pressure.
notes.plans: Push the e-pawn to attack the rook and the king, and use the queen to target multiple weaknesses. If the opponent trades queens, the resulting endgame should still be winning.

notes.explains: In the endgame with a material advantage, the main risks are back rank mate, losing pawns to allow promotion, or stalemate. Here, the player ensures king safety and then uses a ladder mate to finish.
notes.teaches: In winning endgames, prioritize king safety and avoid stalemate traps. Use a ladder mate with queen and rook (or similar) to force checkmate by alternating checks and restricting the king.
notes.plans: Walk the king over, use the rook to cut off the king, and deliver alternating checks to mate.

notes.explains: With a material advantage, the winning side must choose the right move to avoid a stalemate or repetition. Here, the king had several safe squares, but one move allowed a draw by repetition.
notes.teaches: In a winning position, always check for the opponent's possible checks and ensure you have a plan to avoid perpetual check or repetition. Do not automatically retreat to a square that allows the opponent to force a draw.
notes.plans: When ahead, keep the king safe but also keep the initiative; avoid moves that allow the opponent to give perpetual check.

notes.explains: With a material advantage (up a bishop), the goal is to convert. Time pressure is a factor, but a rule of thumb is to avoid a time disadvantage greater than 20%. Trading pieces simplifies the position and increases winning chances.
notes.teaches: When winning, trade pieces to reduce counterplay and simplify to a winning endgame. Manage your clock to avoid panic; a 20% time deficit is a reasonable guideline.
notes.plans: Offer trades, simplify the position, and convert the material advantage by either trading into a winning endgame or checkmating.

notes.explains: White's attempts at counterplay are futile; Black simply takes all the pawns and then pushes the h-pawn and d-pawn. The opponent runs out of moves, and eventually checkmate occurs without needing to promote.
notes.teaches: In a winning endgame, keep pressing by taking all the opponent's pawns and advancing your own. Watch for the opponent's last-ditch counterplay and neutralize it calmly.
notes.plans: Continue to encroach on the opponent's territory, push the pawns, and use the king to support them. The opponent will eventually run out of useful moves.

notes.explains: With a decisive material advantage, the goal is to convert quickly. Two methods are to simplify into a winning endgame or to launch a direct attack on the king. In this position, a mate is possible within a few moves.
