notes.teaches: Follow opening principles: develop knights and bishops, castle early, and avoid premature attacks. Don't try to reinvent the wheel; stick to sound development.
notes.plans: Complete development and castle before starting aggressive actions.

notes.explains: Even though the general rule is not to move the same piece multiple times in the opening, there are exceptions. Here, a free pawn is hanging, and the knight can capture it with no damage to the position, while also gaining access to open squares.
notes.teaches: Learn to recognize when a rule can be broken: if a free pawn is available and the move doesn't harm your position, it's often worth taking, even if it means moving a piece twice.
notes.plans: Take the free pawn with the knight, pressuring the opponent and creating threats.

notes.explains: In this game, the opponent developed the knight to f3 and then to e5, moving the same piece twice without clear benefit. This is an inaccuracy because it loses time and allows the opponent to develop freely. The opponent also blundered a pawn and had a blind spot for a central pawn capture. These mistakes allowed the player to supercharge their position.
notes.teaches: In the opening, avoid moving the same piece twice without a concrete reason. Develop your bishops and knights efficiently, and be alert to central pawn captures. Losing time in the opening can give your opponent a lead in development.
notes.plans: Continue developing pieces and exploiting the opponent's weaknesses, such as the blundered pawn and exposed king.

notes.explains: In queen-pawn openings, the c-pawn and d-pawn often work together to support the center. Keeping the knight behind the c-pawn helps pressure the center. When facing a pawn capture, capturing towards the center is usually best, but sometimes it's fine to keep the tension.
notes.teaches: Understand typical pawn structures in queen-pawn games. When in doubt, capture towards the center, but don't feel obligated to take every offered pawn—maintaining tension can be a valid strategy.
notes.plans: Develop pieces harmoniously, castle, and be ready to recapture if the opponent takes your central pawn.

notes.explains: Both sides have kept pawns in a way that invites captures: you want to recapture and gain central control, while the opponent wants to recapture and bring their knight into play. This standoff means neither side should rush to take.
notes.teaches: In the opening, pawn captures can be double-edged; consider the recapture and resulting piece activity before taking. Sometimes it's better to maintain tension and develop.
notes.plans: Proceed with e3, keeping the tension in the center and developing pieces.

notes.explains: White plays g3 to develop the bishop to g2, but this allows Black to grab more central space with f5. Black instead plays Be6, missing the chance to build a solid pawn center.
notes.teaches: When you have the chance to expand in the center with pawns like f5, do it. Solid pawn formations can be a long-term asset.
notes.plans: Black should consider f5 to gain space and create a strong pawn chain.

notes.explains: Black plays f6, which blocks the knight's natural square and weakens the kingside. The idea is to support the center pawns, but it's premature and creates weaknesses. White then plays c4, a flank attack aiming to undermine the center.
notes.teaches: Avoid weakening pawn moves like f6 early unless necessary; they create permanent weaknesses and hinder piece development. Flank pawn attacks can be used to challenge a strong center, but only if your own development is sound.
notes.plans: White should continue developing pieces and consider exploiting the weakened dark squares around black's king.

notes.explains: Pawns work together as a chain, supporting each other's advances. In this game, black's pawns on e6 and b5 support d5 and c4, creating a strong pawn structure that cramps white's position.
notes.teaches: Use pawns to control the center and gain space, but avoid overextending without proper support.
notes.plans: Build a solid pawn chain and use it to restrict the opponent's pieces while developing your own.

notes.explains: When White plays d4 prematurely, it can lose a pawn if not prepared. The correct way is to prepare with c3 first. If Black captures, the recapture matters: taking with the pawn can open the king and lead to trouble, while the right recapture keeps the position solid.
notes.teaches: In the opening, don't just develop—also consider pawn structure and king safety. When capturing, choose the recapture that keeps your position 'glued shut' and avoids exposing your king.
notes.plans: Recapture in a way that maintains a solid pawn structure and keeps the king safe, then continue development.

notes.explains: White's overextension leaves the c-pawn tender and vulnerable. If that pawn falls, White's position will have serious structural problems.
notes.teaches: Avoid overextending pawns in the opening; a weak pawn can become a long-term target.
notes.plans: Black aims to play c5 to challenge White's center and target the weak c-pawn.

notes.explains: White plays c3, a good move to prepare a break and bring the knight back into play. Black can either take or protect the pawn, but protecting would lead to a damaged structure in the center, so taking is preferable.
notes.teaches: When facing a pawn break, evaluate whether maintaining the pawn is worth structural damage; often it's better to take and keep a sound pawn structure.
notes.plans: Capture on c3 with the b-pawn to keep the structure solid, then continue development with Nf6 or Nf7, and consider the central break d5.

notes.explains: In the Scandinavian, after e4 d5 exd5 Qxd5, Black can also play …e5, which is a different setup. The d- and c-pawns work together to fight against White's central pawns, creating a solid but potentially passive structure.
notes.teaches: Pawn structures in the opening dictate the middlegame plans. The d5 and c6 pawns (or c5 and d5) can form a strong central barrier, but you must ensure your pieces have active squares.
notes.plans: For Black: develop the pieces to natural squares, support the center, and prepare to challenge White's pawns with c5 or e5 breaks when appropriate.

notes.explains: In the Caro-Kann Advance with c5, the diagonal leading to the king is vulnerable to checks and tactics, especially if development is careless. A bishop on b4 can pin the knight on c3, and if the king is exposed, checks can be devastating.
notes.teaches: When playing the Caro-Kann Advance, be extremely careful about the diagonal that can expose your king to checks. Avoid moves that allow your opponent to create threats on this diagonal.
notes.plans: Develop solidly, keep the king safe, and avoid weakening the pawn structure around the center.

notes.explains: In this position, black has a choice to trade on d3 or keep the tension. Trading brings the bishop to a square where it can be a target, but it also simplifies. Keeping the tension and developing is also fine, especially at lower levels.
notes.teaches: When facing a central pawn exchange, consider both options: trading can simplify but may give the opponent a target; keeping the tension maintains flexibility and avoids helping your opponent develop.
notes.plans: If not trading, develop pieces naturally, castle, and prepare to challenge the center.

notes.explains: The position has transformed into a French Defense-like structure with a locked center. Black has a weak pawn on b5 that can be targeted with b3.
notes.teaches: In locked positions, look for weaknesses in the opponent's pawn structure. A move like b3 can undermine the support of a weak pawn, creating tactical opportunities.
notes.plans: White should aim to exploit the weak pawn, possibly by playing b3 and then taking on b5. Black must avoid getting into a 'grappling match' that allows white to win material.

notes.explains: In queen's pawn games, the d-pawn is protected twice and the c-pawn is protected twice, so a single pawn push doesn't pressure the center. In king's pawn games, the e-pawn is protected once and supported by the queen, making central play different.
notes.teaches: Understand the structural differences between queen's pawn and king's pawn openings. In queen's pawn games, the d and c pawns should advance together to support each other.
notes.plans: In a queen's pawn game, aim to develop pieces while preparing to advance the c-pawn to support the d-pawn.

notes.explains: When you have a material advantage, the opponent's threats are often less dangerous than they appear. You can often ignore them and continue improving your position, as long as you have a clear path to safety.
notes.teaches: When you are winning, don't panic over every threat. Calculate the opponent's resources and see if you can simply continue with your own plan, especially if you can maintain the material edge.
notes.plans: Keep the material advantage, avoid unnecessary risks, and look for ways to simplify or increase the pressure.

notes.explains: The player had a material advantage but had to be careful not to blunder. The opponent was stalling, but the player needed to coordinate rooks and win pawns while avoiding checks.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, simplify the position and trade pieces to reach a winning endgame. Keep your king safe and avoid unnecessary risks.
notes.plans: Coordinate your rooks, target weak pawns, and gradually convert the advantage without allowing counterplay.

notes.explains: After the opponent makes a serious blunder (hanging a queen), Black is up a queen. The instructor emphasizes using the extra material actively: bring the queen into play, create forks, and trade pieces to simplify into a winning endgame. Even sacrificing material like a rook for a knight is acceptable when you have a huge advantage.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, activate your pieces and use them to create threats. Simplify the position by trading pieces, but keep your queen active to maintain pressure. Don't be afraid to give back some material if it leads to a faster win.
notes.plans: Use the queen to fork pieces, win more material, and then trade down to a winning endgame. Keep the initiative and avoid unnecessary risks.

notes.explains: The opponent has lost two pieces for a pawn, and now they are trying to take something back. This is a common reaction, but it often leads to further losses.
notes.teaches: When you are winning material, don't panic if the opponent tries to complicate. Keep your pieces protected and continue to press your advantage.
notes.plans: Protect your pieces, avoid hanging material, and continue to develop.

notes.explains: In a position with a six-point material advantage, the game is effectively decided; the remaining pieces are few, so there is little danger of a tactical accident.
notes.teaches: When you are up significant material, simplify and avoid unnecessary risks; do not allow one-move blunders to squander the advantage.
notes.plans: Activate the king toward the center to support pawns, and bring rooks to central files to prepare a pawn push.

notes.explains: In this position, the side with a material advantage must still be precise; a single inaccurate move can turn a winning position into an equal one or even a losing one. The evaluation swings wildly based on specific moves, showing that concrete calculation matters more than the abstract material count.
notes.teaches: Always check for forcing moves like checks and captures before settling on a plan. A move that looks natural may allow a perpetual check or a tactical resource that nullifies your advantage.
notes.plans: When you are winning, look for the most forcing continuation to convert, and avoid moves that give the opponent counterplay.

notes.explains: In this chaotic middlegame, both sides have multiple hanging pieces, and the position is far more complex than expected. The player is up material but must navigate tactical threats while managing the clock.
notes.teaches: When the position is wildly tactical and you are ahead in material, simplify by trading pieces or forcing favorable exchanges, rather than trying to calculate every variation.
notes.plans: Consider queen moves that maintain the material advantage while creating threats, such as queen to g3 or h3, and look for pins or forks to consolidate.

notes.explains: When up material, it's important to use your advantage by activating all your pieces and avoiding unnecessary risks. Taking extra pawns can open lines for the opponent to counterattack.
notes.teaches: In a winning position, prioritize safety and piece activity over greed. Avoid opening lines that give the opponent counterplay.
notes.plans: Bring your remaining pieces into the attack, and consider pawn breaks that restrict the opponent's pieces while advancing your own.

notes.explains: After winning a pawn, the opponent panicked and sacrificed material instead of following a logical plan, which was a mistake.
notes.teaches: When you are down material, avoid desperate sacrifices; instead, find the most resilient defensive setup and try to create counterplay.
notes.plans: If you are material down, consolidate your position, trade pieces if possible, and avoid further weakening your position.

notes.explains: Trading queens and pieces when you have a material advantage reduces the opponent's attacking chances and simplifies the game.
notes.teaches: When you are up material, aim to trade pieces to neutralize counterplay and convert your advantage.
notes.plans: Continue trading pieces and simplify the position to reach a winning endgame.

notes.explains: In a position with a large material advantage, playing passively can cause you to miss tactical opportunities. Here, a check that forks the king and rook wins material on the spot, but there is also a tactical idea with a bishop sacrifice leading to a fork.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, look for active moves that create threats. Don't play passively; seek checks, captures, and tactics to increase your advantage.
notes.plans: Play the check that wins the rook, or if that is not available, consider the bishop sacrifice to set up a fork on f7.

notes.explains: After winning three pawns, the position is winning, but you must remain careful. The best move is often the most forcing one, like blocking a check with a pawn that also attacks a piece.
notes.teaches: When ahead material, prefer forcing moves that maintain the initiative and increase the pressure, rather than passive defense.
notes.plans: Continue developing, castle, and avoid allowing counterplay. If the opponent offers a queen trade, consider it to simplify into a winning endgame.

notes.explains: When you are up three pawns, the priority is to consolidate and trade pieces to simplify into a winning endgame. Playing normal developing moves and offering trades is a solid approach, but if the opponent has weakened their king, you can also consider a direct attack.
notes.teaches: Material advantage should be converted by trading down and avoiding complications. However, if the opponent's king is exposed, an attack can be even more effective.
notes.plans: If the opponent has a weak king, consider attacking. Otherwise, trade pieces and simplify to a won endgame.

notes.explains: With an extra rook, the priority is to trade pieces, especially rooks, to simplify into a winning endgame. Also, avoid knight forks by not moving into forking squares.
notes.teaches: When ahead in material, trade pieces to reduce counterplay; be wary of enemy knight forks.
notes.plans: Aim to exchange rooks, and if a knight is attacked, give it an escape square with a rook move.

notes.explains: In this position, White has accumulated a two-pawn advantage and is simplifying, while Black's position is passive and lacks counterplay. The key is to maintain the advantage without taking unnecessary risks.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, keep the position simple and avoid complications that could give your opponent counterplay. Convert your advantage methodically.
notes.plans: Continue to trade pieces and pawns, activate the king in the endgame, and use the extra pawns to create a passed pawn or force weaknesses.

notes.explains: When you have an extra piece, you want to open the position to increase its value. Here, a pawn trade was initiated to create open lines.
notes.teaches: Material advantage often favors open positions; use pawn breaks to trade pawns and activate your pieces.
notes.plans: Look for pawn trades that open files and diagonals for your pieces.

notes.explains: In this position, after a queen check, taking the queen would lead to a trade, but sacrificing a rook allows winning a knight because it is undefended. The exchange sacrifice results in a material advantage of a rook for a bishop and knight.
notes.teaches: When a piece is overloaded or undefended, consider sacrificing material to win a more valuable piece or to gain a decisive material advantage.
notes.plans: Continue converting the material advantage by simplifying and trading down to a winning endgame.

notes.explains: When you are up a piece, giving up a pawn is acceptable if it maintains your advantage and avoids worse threats. The opponent's move that wins a pawn may also expose their king, preventing castling and leaving it in the center.
notes.teaches: When ahead in material, prioritize king safety and activity over preserving every pawn. Look for the opponent's threats against your own king before grabbing material.
notes.plans: If the opponent exposes their king, keep the pressure on the center and prepare to exploit the king's vulnerability with checks and attacks.

notes.explains: In this position, White has a queen and a pawn against two minor pieces, which is a material advantage, but the queen must be preserved and the king must have an escape square to avoid back-rank mate threats.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, prioritize king safety and piece coordination over greed; a queen is powerful but vulnerable if trapped.
notes.plans: White should aim to consolidate by creating luft (e.g., a3) and possibly trade off pieces to simplify into a winning endgame, while ensuring the king has a getaway.

notes.explains: With the queen alone against several well-coordinated enemy pieces, the side with more pieces has a decisive advantage. The lone queen cannot defend against multiple threats.
notes.teaches: Material superiority matters when the opponent's pieces are active. Use your extra pieces to create threats that overload the enemy queen.

notes.explains: When you've won a piece early, you should be willing to trade queens to simplify into a winning endgame. Castling is important, but if there's a free pawn, taking it is fine once the queens are off.
notes.teaches: In the opening, if you're up material, trade pieces to reduce counterplay. Don't be afraid to take free pawns when your king is safe and the queen trade is available.
notes.plans: Castle kingside, then take the free pawn on d4, and if the opponent tries to pin with Bg5, you can ignore it or even provoke the trade of bishops.

notes.explains: The opponent has only one rook, so there is no counterplay. The material advantage is overwhelming, and the rooks can infiltrate the opponent's position.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, simplify the position and use your rooks to penetrate the opponent's camp. Avoid unnecessary risks and convert methodically.
notes.plans: Trade rooks if possible, then use the remaining rook to infiltrate the seventh rank or the opponent's back rank, creating threats and winning more material.

notes.explains: When you are already winning material, simplifying is a reliable way to convert. Trading pieces reduces the opponent's counterplay and makes your advantage easier to realize.
notes.teaches: If you are up material, be happy to trade pieces, especially active ones. Each exchange removes potential threats from the opponent.
notes.plans: Continue developing and castle, then aim to trade off more pieces while maintaining your extra material.

notes.explains: In this position, Black has a material advantage (up a pawn) and a good position, but the opponent is defending accurately. The immediate tactical threats and the placement of pieces are changing rapidly, so careful calculation is needed.
notes.teaches: When you are better, do not rush to force matters; instead, consolidate your advantage by improving your pieces and maintaining pressure while avoiding unnecessary risks.
notes.plans: Castle to safety, then aim to place the knight on a strong central outpost like d5, and prepare to exploit the opponent's weaknesses.

notes.explains: When you have a material advantage, trading pieces reduces the opponent's counterplay and makes your advantage easier to convert. Even in a winning position, you must be careful not to lose your own pieces.
notes.teaches: In a winning position, trade pieces to simplify, but always keep your own pieces safe. The fewer pieces the opponent has, the fewer chances they have for tactics.
notes.plans: Look for favorable trades, especially of major pieces, and head towards a winning endgame.

notes.explains: Trading pieces is simple and effective when you are ahead. The opponent cannot do anything without pieces.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, trade pieces to reduce the opponent's counterplay and make the win easier.
notes.plans: Trade bishops, knights, and queens if possible.

notes.explains: After winning material, the game plan is to simplify by trading pieces. With a large material advantage, trading down reduces the opponent's counterplay and leads to a winning endgame.
notes.teaches: When you are ahead in material, the simplest winning method is to exchange pieces, not pawns. This reduces the opponent's attacking chances and makes your advantage easier to convert.
notes.plans: Look for opportunities to trade pieces while maintaining your material edge. In the endgame, activate your king and use your extra pawns to create passed pawns.

notes.explains: In a winning position, choose the most practical and cleanest continuation, even if there are flashier tactical options.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, simplifying by trading queens can remove all counterplay and lead to an easy win.
notes.plans: If you can trade queens and maintain a material lead, do so; then use your extra material to convert the endgame.

notes.explains: White trades queens anyway, removing their main attacking piece. Black should immediately recapture, but instead declines the trade, allowing White to improve. Black then finds a good check with queen takes e5, but White correctly blocks with the bishop instead of moving the king, keeping the rook safe.
notes.teaches: When you are ahead in material, you should welcome trades, especially of queens, to simplify into a winning endgame. Also, when in check, consider blocking with a piece if it also develops or protects other pieces, rather than moving the king.
notes.plans: Black should take the queen, castle queenside, and slowly convert the material advantage by trading pawns and activating the rooks.

notes.explains: The opponent's moves are solid but not threatening. A move like Ne5 is cool but has no threat, so it can be ignored. The position is still winning, so simplifying by trading rooks is a safe way to proceed.
notes.teaches: When you are winning, avoid unnecessary complications. Simplify the position by trading pieces, but always be alert to tactical tricks like forks.
notes.plans: Trade rooks, keep the queen active, and avoid blundering a fork. If the opponent plays Nh4, consider taking the rook and then dealing with the knight.

notes.explains: The pawn on c4 is tempting, but taking it feels wrong because it doesn't fit the position's spirit and there may be a refutation. Instead, offering a queen trade with queen d8 reduces stress and leads to a long-term static advantage.
notes.teaches: Sometimes the best move is to simplify and trade queens when you have a structural advantage, rather than grabbing material that could backfire. Long-term static play can be more reliable than risky tactics.
notes.plans: Play queen d8 to offer a queen trade, then if accepted, proceed to the endgame with a better pawn structure.

notes.explains: We have a choice to win material: either take a free pawn or trade into a favorable endgame with bishop and knight versus rook. The latter is a practical endgame that is winning with correct technique.
notes.teaches: In winning positions, simplify to a known winning endgame when possible; converting a material advantage requires technique, so choose the path you know how to win.
notes.plans: Simplify by trading rooks, then use the bishop and knight to create threats and win the rook or promote a pawn.

notes.explains: When you have a material advantage, simplifying trades reduces the opponent's counterplay. Moves like Bg5 pinning and taking a knight, or trading pieces, make it harder for the opponent to create problems.
notes.teaches: In a winning position, trade pieces to decrease the opponent's activity and make the win easier.
notes.plans: Look for trades that remove the opponent's active pieces, then bring all your pieces to the attack.

notes.explains: When you are up material, simplifying by trading pieces is often a good strategy. Here, White chooses to trade pieces to reduce Black's counterplay, even though other defensive moves were possible.
notes.teaches: When ahead in material, look to exchange pieces to increase your advantage. This reduces the opponent's attacking chances and makes your extra pawns more significant.
notes.plans: Continue to trade pieces while maintaining a safe position, then convert the extra pawns in the endgame.

notes.explains: When you have a material advantage, trading pieces simplifies the position and reduces counterplay. Here, trading rooks is a huge win because it removes attacking pieces and makes the win easier.
notes.teaches: In a winning position, trade pieces to simplify and reduce the opponent's chances. Doubling rooks on an open file can increase pressure before trading.
notes.plans: Trade rooks, then use the remaining pieces to hunt pawns and promote.

notes.explains: After the opponent's king is stuck in the center, White has a choice between aggressive moves like knight e5, which attacks multiple pieces, or simpler moves that remove counterplay.
notes.teaches: Sometimes the simplest move is the best. By removing the opponent's counterplay, you make your own plan easier to execute. Avoid giving the opponent chances to activate their pieces.
notes.plans: Play a simple move like knight to c3 to prevent Black from getting counterplay. Then proceed with the plan of controlling the g-file, bringing the king to the center, and advancing pawns in the endgame.

notes.explains: When the opponent creates a counterattack against your king, you don't have to rush in with the knight. Instead, you can trade pieces to simplify into a better endgame, especially if you have a material advantage.
notes.teaches: In winning positions, trading down reduces the opponent's counterplay and increases your advantage. Simplify when you are ahead.
notes.plans: Continue trading pieces, especially if it wins material or exposes the opponent's king.

notes.explains: A piece that ventures deep into enemy territory can become trapped if its escape squares are covered. It's important to attack such pieces and also to see the correct way to trap them.
notes.teaches: When an enemy piece is deep in your position, don't be shy about attacking it. Look for the move that cuts off all its escape squares, not just the obvious one.
notes.plans: Use your pieces to surround the trapped piece and win it, or force the opponent to lose material to save it.

notes.explains: Black plays ...g6, which threatens to trap the bishop on h4. White must decide whether to sacrifice the bishop or retreat it to maintain material balance.
notes.teaches: Be alert to tactics that trap your pieces. Sometimes a sacrifice can be justified for an attack, but often it's better to retreat and keep the position stable.
notes.plans: Retreat the bishop to defend the knight, and if the knight is taken, recapture with the pawn to maintain a pawn duo that can push forward.

notes.explains: White's rook is trapped on an open diagonal, and a move like Bd5 or Qd5 would win it. Instead, white plays a4, a pointless pawn move that ignores the threat.
notes.teaches: Always look for forcing moves and threats. If your opponent has a hanging piece, exploit it before making quiet moves.
notes.plans: White should have played a move that attacks the trapped rook, such as Bd5 or Qd5, to win material.

notes.explains: When you have a material advantage, you can often ignore a hanging piece and instead create a counterattack that is even stronger. This requires seeing the opponent's threats and finding a better move.
notes.teaches: In a winning position, don't always grab material. Sometimes the best move is to create a bigger threat, forcing the opponent to respond and lose more.
notes.plans: Look for counterattacks that win more material or force a favorable trade.

notes.explains: In a chaotic middlegame with both kings exposed, the immediate recapture or obvious check is not always best; here a counterattack on the knight with the queen was stronger than a check that allowed the opponent to gain tempo.
notes.teaches: When under attack, look for counterattacks that hit the opponent's pieces with tempo, rather than automatically defending or checking. This can turn the tables and force the opponent to react.
notes.plans: After the counterattack, if the opponent takes the bishop, continue the attack with the remaining pieces, focusing on the king.

notes.explains: If White had not played pawn takes d5 and instead threatened the rook, black could have counterattacked. If White then takes the rook, black might have perpetual check, leading to a draw. The only way for White to survive is to bring the rook to the second rank to protect the king, but then the queen is behind enemy lines with a material advantage but not necessarily winning.
notes.teaches: Counterattacks are part of the game. When you have a material advantage, be careful not to allow perpetual check. Look for defensive resources like bringing a rook to the second rank to shield the king.
notes.plans: If you find yourself in a similar situation, prioritize king safety and avoid allowing perpetual check, even if it means giving back some material.

notes.explains: When both a bishop and a knight are under attack, the natural reaction is to save one, but a better idea is to create a counterattack. Moving the bishop to e4, defended by the knight, saves the piece and creates threats. Alternatively, queen a5 attacks the rook and creates a mating threat because the queen and knight converge on f7.
notes.teaches: In tactical positions, before saving a piece, look for checks, captures, and attacks. A counterattack can save material and create a decisive threat.
notes.plans: Play queen a5, attacking the rook and threatening mate on f7, forcing the opponent to deal with the immediate threat.

notes.explains: When the opponent tries to open lines on the side where your king is not, you can often turn the tables. By using the rook to counterattack along the opened file, you reverse the pressure onto the opponent.
notes.teaches: Counterattacking on the open file can be more effective than defending passively. This 'judo' reversal exploits the opponent's overextension.
notes.plans: Look for opportunities to switch the direction of attack when the opponent's king is exposed on the other side.

notes.explains: When the opponent launches a king attack, it's crucial to stay calm and check if the threats are real. Counterattacking the attacking pieces can be more effective than passive defense.
notes.teaches: Don't panic when facing a potential mate. Calculate the exact threats and look for counterplay, such as attacking the opponent's key pieces.
notes.plans: If the opponent's attack is not decisive, counterattack their pieces to force trades or gain time.

notes.explains: The game featured counter-attacking play: when the opponent attacked, the speaker created threats of their own, such as a check that forced the opponent to abandon an attack.
notes.teaches: In chess, a strong counterattack can neutralize an opponent's initiative. Look for checks and captures that create threats while defending.
notes.plans: If the opponent attacks your piece, consider whether you can create a bigger threat, like a check or a fork, rather than just retreating.

notes.explains: When the opponent's queen is out early, a strong counterattack can be launched by sacrificing a pawn (d4) to open lines and develop pieces rapidly.
notes.teaches: If the opponent brings their queen out early, consider pawn sacrifices to open lines and develop pieces with tempo, aiming for a powerful attack.
notes.plans: After d4, if the queen takes, develop with tempo and aim to castle long, having all pieces active.

notes.explains: The position is incredibly sharp, and the best move for White is a counterattacking pawn break in the center, opening lines against the exposed king. The immediate capture and recapture lead to a position where a knight sacrifice is the only winning continuation, because it exposes the enemy king and wins material back.
notes.teaches: In wild tactical positions, the most forcing move is not always the best. Sometimes you must sacrifice material to maintain the initiative and expose the enemy king. Look for moves that create threats that are more important than the material you give up.
notes.plans: After the knight sacrifice, White continues to harass the king and eventually wins the queen, but the resulting material balance is still complex, so accurate play is required to convert.

notes.explains: In rook endgames, placing your rook on the opponent's second rank is a powerful way to restrict their king and attack their pawns from behind. This is a key winning technique.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, aim to put your rook on the enemy's second rank. It cuts off the king and creates threats against the pawns.
notes.plans: Get the rook to the second rank, then use it to win pawns and promote.

notes.explains: In the rook endgame, Black has a bishop while White does not, which is a decisive advantage. The plan is to win pawns with the rook and also try to trade rooks to reach a winning bishop vs. pawns endgame.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, king activity, rook infiltration, and putting the rook behind passed pawns are key. Also, trading rooks when you have a minor piece advantage can simplify to a win.
notes.plans: Use the rook to pick up pawns, and if possible, trade rooks to enter a winning bishop endgame.

notes.explains: In the resulting endgame, the two rooks and a passed pawn are sufficient to win because the enemy king is cut off and cannot participate.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, active rooks on the seventh rank and a passed pawn can be decisive, especially when the enemy king is confined.
notes.plans: Keep the rooks active, push the passed pawn, and use the rooks to cut off the enemy king.

notes.explains: In this winning rook endgame, White has no counterplay and is reduced to passive moves. The key is to keep the rook centralized and protected while advancing pawns, and to bring the king into the action.
notes.teaches: When converting a won endgame, prioritize king activity and pawn advancement, but always be ready to defend your pawns. Avoid unnecessary pawn pushes that create weaknesses.
notes.plans: Bring the king to the center, keep the rook active, and push the passed pawns. If the opponent tries to create counterplay, be prepared to trade or defend.

notes.explains: In a rook endgame with a two-pawn majority, the winning method is to push the majority pawns with the rook supporting from behind. This deflects the enemy rook and allows the king to assist in promoting a pawn.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, use your majority to create a passed pawn. Place your rook behind the pawn to support its advance, and bring your king to help escort it.
notes.plans: Push the majority pawns, keep the rook behind them, and bring the king up to support the pawn's promotion.

notes.explains: After a series of moves, the position simplifies to a rook endgame with a four-versus-three pawn majority on one side. This is winning for the side with the majority.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, a pawn majority on one side can be a decisive advantage. Active rook play and creating a passed pawn are key.
notes.plans: White should advance the pawn majority to create a passed pawn, while keeping the rook active to support it.

notes.explains: White made a mistake by attacking a pawn with the rook, losing a pawn to the attack, and then failing to defend the passed pawn properly, allowing it to be captured.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, do not trade a pawn to attack a pawn if it loses your advantage; prioritize defending your passed pawn and maintaining material superiority.
notes.plans: White should have defended the passed pawn with the rook from behind or the side, and used the king to support it, rather than going pawn hunting.

notes.explains: In an endgame with an extra pawn, the plan is to create a weakness in the opponent's camp, such as a pawn that must be defended by the king, and then double rooks on the open file to increase pressure.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, active rooks and creating a target are key. Double rooks on the seventh rank or on an open file can tie down the opponent and lead to decisive material gains.
notes.plans: Play to double rooks on the d-file, target the weak pawn, and be ready to exploit the opponent's king being tied to defense.

notes.explains: In rook endgames, the defender's king is often tied to stopping passed pawns, so the attacker should coordinate all pieces—rooks, king, and pawns—to advance together and create threats.
notes.teaches: Coordinate your entire army in endgames: bring the king up, advance pawns as a group, and use the rook to infiltrate. This collective pressure is more effective than piece-meal attacks.
notes.plans: If the opponent plays a passive rook move like Rf1, respond by advancing your king and pawns, preparing to target weaknesses. If they push a pawn, centralize your king and prepare to exploit the resulting weaknesses.

notes.explains: In the rook endgame, Black's king was exposed and White gave checks that only helped Black's king advance to a safer, more active square. The checks were not part of a plan and just improved Black's king position.
notes.teaches: Do not give checks in endgames just for the sake of checking. Each check should have a purpose, such as driving the king to a worse square or gaining time for a useful move.
notes.plans: In rook endgames, focus on activating your king, cutting off the opponent's king, and creating passed pawns rather than aimless checks.

notes.explains: In a rook endgame with a material advantage, the winning method is to place the rook behind the passed pawn and use the king to support its advance. The opponent's best defense is to put their rook behind the pawn or push it as far as possible.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, the rule is: rook behind the passed pawn. Use the king to escort the pawn, and if you have a pawn majority, you can often win by creating a passed pawn.
notes.plans: Advance the pawn with the rook behind it, bring the king up to support, and if the opponent is tied down, use the rook to gobble up their pawns.

notes.explains: In a rook endgame, simplification is often the fastest way to win. By trading pieces, the game becomes a pure pawn race where connected passed pawns are decisive.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, simplifying to a pawn endgame can be a winning technique if you have connected passed pawns. Evaluate trades carefully to ensure they lead to a won pawn endgame.
notes.plans: Trade rooks if it leads to a winning pawn endgame. Then push the connected passed pawns together, using the king to support.

notes.explains: In the resulting endgame, white is winning because the rook on a7 and the passed pawns are faster than black's counterplay. The race is in white's favor.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, activity and the speed of passed pawns are crucial. Evaluate which side's pawns are faster and whether the rook can support them effectively.
notes.plans: Push the g-pawn and use the rook to support it, while keeping the black king cut off.

notes.explains: A rook on the opponent's second rank restricts their king to the back rank and attacks their pawns. Even if the rook is attacked, keeping it there can be stronger than retreating.
notes.teaches: When you have a rook on the seventh rank, consider maintaining it even under attack, as it can create mating threats and win material.
notes.plans: Use the rook to confine the king, bring other pieces to deliver checkmate without promoting a pawn.

notes.explains: In the endgame, the player has an extra knight and two pawns. They aim to activate their rook and place it on the seventh rank, which is a dominant position that often leads to victory.
notes.teaches: A rook on the seventh rank is a classic endgame advantage: it attacks pawns from the side and restricts the enemy king. Prioritize getting your rook there.
notes.plans: Use checks to force the king to a bad square, then bring the rook to the seventh rank. If the opponent defends, look for forks or other tactics to win more material.

notes.explains: In the endgame, a rook on the seventh rank (or second rank for the defender) is extremely powerful because it attacks all the pawns from the side and restricts the enemy king.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, aim to plant your rook on the seventh rank to attack pawns and create threats. The king can also be used aggressively to support the rook.
notes.plans: Get the rook to the seventh rank, attack the pawns, and use the king to support the advance.

notes.explains: With a material advantage, the conversion is straightforward if you are methodical. Placing a rook on the seventh rank attacks all the pawns, and trading rooks simplifies the win.
notes.teaches: In winning endgames, activate your rooks, put them on the seventh rank to create threats, and aim to trade pieces to reach a simple pawn-up endgame.
notes.plans: Put a rook on the second rank (seventh for White) to attack pawns, then trade rooks to simplify, and push the queenside pawns.

notes.explains: Playing the king's pawn (e4) is more aggressive than the queen's pawn because it opens lines for both the queen and the bishop, enabling early queen sorties. However, bringing the queen out early can be weak if the opponent has no weaknesses.
notes.teaches: Early queen development is only effective when it targets weaknesses (like f7/f2) or gains time. Otherwise, the queen becomes a target and the opponent gains development.
notes.plans: If the opponent plays an early queen move, respond by developing pieces and preparing to attack the queen, while also aiming for central pawn breaks.

notes.explains: When the opponent plays an early queen move, you can often seize the initiative by attacking the queen and gaining time. In this position, playing c5 invites the pawn trade, but the best move is to take the pawn if it cannot recapture.
notes.teaches: If a pawn can be captured and cannot be recaptured, it is often best to take it, as it gives you a central pawn majority and easy development.
notes.plans: After taking the pawn, aim to establish two pawns in the center and develop pieces quickly, exploiting the opponent's misplaced queen.

notes.explains: In this clustered position, the only check (queen to a5) is not forcing because it can be easily counterattacked, so it lacks a clear plan. Captures are better, but one capture is more forcing than the other: capturing a piece that attacks the queen forces white to respond, whereas a simple capture allows white any move.
notes.teaches: When choosing moves, prioritize checks, captures, and threats, but evaluate how forcing each is. A move that attacks the queen is more forcing than a plain capture because it limits the opponent's options.
notes.plans: After the forcing capture, black would have three attackers on the center, win a pawn, and then establish two center pawns, develop the bishop, and castle.

notes.explains: When two knights are tied to defending each other and other pieces, they become vulnerable to tactics like a bishop landing on e5, which hits multiple targets at once.
notes.teaches: Look for forcing moves (checks, captures, attacks) that overload the opponent's pieces; if several pieces are tied up, a single move can win material.
notes.plans: Play the most forcing move available, such as bishop to e5, to exploit the opponent's coordination.

notes.explains: Before castling, you must check for forcing moves for the opponent. In this position, if white castles, black can play Qd4+ forking the king and the unprotected bishop, winning material.
notes.teaches: Always scan for your opponent's forcing moves—checks, captures, threats—even if they are not immediately obvious. This habit is essential to avoid blunders and progress beyond 1200.
notes.plans: Instead of castling, white should first defend the bishop with a move like Be2, which also prepares long castling, or move the king to safety.

notes.explains: Black plays f6 to attack the knight, which looks natural, but White responds with a bizarre king move (Ke1), which is not a computer move and seems to have no clear purpose. Black then takes the knight, but White has a tactical resource: Bf7+ winning the queen.
notes.teaches: When your opponent makes a strange move, look for forcing moves—checks, captures, and attacks—to punish them. Even if a move looks natural, it may be a mistake if it doesn't address the opponent's threats.
notes.plans: White should capitalize on the tactic to win the queen, while Black must try to minimize the damage and find active piece play.

notes.explains: In this winning position, there are multiple good moves, but the best is rook takes a7, which is checkmate. The opponent is stalling by thinking long before the mate, which is poor etiquette.
notes.teaches: When you have a winning tactic, look for the most forcing and efficient finish, such as a checkmate, rather than prolonging the game.
notes.plans: Deliver the checkmate with rook takes a7, ending the game immediately.

notes.explains: White has a chance to seize an advantage by playing the most forcing moves. The hierarchy of forcing moves is: checks (attacks on the king), captures, and attacks on valuable pieces like the queen.
notes.teaches: When you have a lead in development, look for the most forcing continuation—checks, captures, and threats—to maintain the initiative and prevent your opponent from consolidating.
notes.plans: White should consider moves like Bxf7+ (a check) or e5 (attacking the queen) to rip open the center and launch an attack against the exposed black king.

notes.explains: The opponent played a move that removed the defender of a key piece, a 'superseding concept' where a forcing move disrupts the opponent's defense. The player had to calculate the opponent's most forcing response, which was a queen check, and realize that the position was actually fine for black despite the scary appearance.
notes.teaches: When you have a forcing move, you must calculate your opponent's most forcing replies. A move that seems to lose material might be fine if you see the defensive resources.
notes.plans: After the forcing sequence, develop pieces and maintain the initiative. Do not panic if the position looks dangerous; trust your calculation.

notes.explains: In this sharp attacking position, the opponent's king is exposed and the attacker has multiple threats. The defender is often forced to take or block, with no real alternatives, making the attack nearly unstoppable if calculated correctly.
notes.teaches: When you have a strong attack, look for forcing moves that give the opponent no choice. If every reply is forced, you can calculate the attack to a clear result.
notes.plans: Continue the attack by bringing the queen and knight into the attack, aiming for mate or material gain.

notes.explains: The best move here was knight to b4, punishing the queen for coming out early and setting up a fork with bishop and knight. This is a concrete tactic that is hard to see but very strong.
notes.teaches: When the opponent brings their queen out early, look for ways to punish it with knight forks or discovered attacks. Even if a move is not obvious, it may be the best if it exploits the queen's poor placement.
notes.plans: If white plays knight a3, black can play queen a5, setting up an unstoppable discovered attack on the knight.

notes.explains: The fishing pole (or fish hook) is a trap where you offer a piece (like a knight on g5) to an opponent who has castled, while you have not (or vice versa), to open lines for a rook and queen attack on the king. In this example, taking the knight is not required, and even if taken, black can win with queen a5 check and mate first.
notes.teaches: Recognize the fishing pole pattern: a rook on the h-file, a queen and knight setup, and a piece on g5 to bait. But remember, you don't have to take the bait; you can decline and still be winning.
notes.plans: If the opponent takes the knight, black should find queen a5 check and then mate before white can mate.

notes.explains: In a queen's gambit declined variation, similar fishing pole ideas can arise: after castling, e3, h6, h4, the opponent may try to bait you into taking on h4, but the queen and rook snipe from a distance. You don't have to take.
notes.teaches: Be aware of pawn pushes like h4 in the opening that may be traps. You can decline the bait and maintain a solid position.
notes.plans: If the opponent offers a queen trade or plays a quiet move, black can trade queens and play simply down a pawn, bringing the rook to the middle and developing the light-squared bishop to fight back against the pawn.

notes.explains: In the Caro-Kann, after the exchange of pawns, the plan is straightforward: develop the knights and bishops and castle. A move like blocking the bishop with a pawn is non-traditional because it hinders piece development.
notes.teaches: Prioritize development and castling in the opening. Avoid moves that block your own pieces without clear compensation.
notes.plans: Develop the knight to f6, the light-squared bishop to f5, the dark-squared bishop to g7, and castle kingside.

notes.explains: When the opponent makes unusual moves, like a knight zigzagging, there is no immediate threat. Panicking and playing a defensive pawn move like e6 is unnecessary; instead, continue developing.
notes.teaches: Do not overreact to odd moves. Stick to your development plan unless there is a concrete threat.
notes.plans: Continue developing the light-squared bishop and prepare to play e6, then develop the dark-squared bishop and castle.

notes.explains: In this position, Black has reasonable developing moves like a knight or the light-squared bishop, but knight to d7 is poor because it blocks the bishop.
notes.teaches: Avoid developing pieces to squares that block your own pieces, especially bishops.
notes.plans: Develop harmoniously, keeping lines open for all pieces.

notes.explains: Black's c6 and then recapturing with the knight is the natural way to continue the gambit, but black is still down a pawn. White's position is comfortable with fast development and a healthy pawn structure.
notes.teaches: When you sacrifice a pawn, you must develop rapidly and create threats to compensate. If the opponent can consolidate, your gambit has failed.
notes.plans: White should focus on solid development and keeping the extra pawn, while black needs to find active piece play.

notes.explains: The opponent's setup leaves a knight passive and a bishop blocked, mirroring a familiar structure. White's development is slow, giving Black time to complete development without pressure.
notes.teaches: Recognize when the opponent's pieces are poorly placed; if they are not creating threats, you can develop calmly and aim for a favorable pawn break in the center.
notes.plans: Finish development, then play the central pawn break (e5) to challenge White's structure and open lines.

notes.explains: When the opponent pushes flank pawns early instead of developing pieces, they leave the king exposed and their pieces at home. This gives the developed side a clear target.
notes.teaches: Develop all your pieces before starting pawn pushes, especially on the flanks. If your opponent neglects development, focus your pieces on their king.
notes.plans: Keep the bishop pointed at the king, play rook to g1 to create direct threats, and prepare to open lines with pawn breaks like e5.

notes.explains: Black has developed four pieces while White has only pawns out, so White's position is already uncomfortable. The move c5 to trap the bishop fails because of a check, allowing the bishop to retreat to e5 and win material.
notes.teaches: Development matters: getting pieces out quickly is crucial, and trying to win a piece with a pawn move can backfire if the opponent has tactical resources like checks.
notes.plans: White should focus on completing development and avoiding pawn moves that create weaknesses without gaining an advantage.

notes.explains: In the Dutch Defense, Stonewall setup, the player develops the knight to the center and the bishop to a long diagonal, which is better than developing to a passive square. The opponent's pawns have advanced, so the knight cannot be attacked by them, creating a potential outpost.
notes.teaches: In the opening, develop pieces to active squares, especially central outposts that cannot be easily chased away by pawns. A bishop on a long diagonal is often better than a passive one.
notes.plans: Look for opportunities to place a knight on an outpost square in the opponent's territory, supported by your own pawns.

notes.explains: When the opponent attacks a knight, the simplest defense is often to move it while continuing development. Missing a free pawn because of autopilot is common at lower levels.
notes.teaches: Always scan for free material, but don't let it distract from sound development. If a pawn is truly free, take it when it doesn't compromise your position.
notes.plans: Continue developing pieces and castle early to ensure king safety.

notes.explains: When the opponent's bishop eyes your center pawn, it's important to finish development and castle. If the opponent's pieces are already active on one side, you can castle to the other side to avoid immediate pressure.
notes.teaches: Prioritize king safety and development. Choose the castling side that avoids the opponent's active pieces.
notes.plans: Develop the bishop, support the center, and castle to the side away from the opponent's threats.

notes.explains: When the opponent makes random pawn moves like a5-a4, they are wasting time. White has developed three pieces to Black's zero, giving a clear lead in development.
notes.teaches: Don't be distracted by irrelevant pawn moves; stick to your opening plan and continue developing. A lead in development is a tangible advantage.
notes.plans: Continue developing pieces and prepare to castle.

notes.explains: In the Caro-Kann structure, black often develops the bishop to f5, plays e6, and later moves the knight to e7. This solid setup prepares to castle and complete development.
notes.teaches: In the Caro-Kann, a typical development plan is bishop to f5, e6, and knight to e7, which solidifies the position and prepares to castle.
notes.plans: Black should develop pieces harmoniously, aiming to castle quickly and then decide on further plans based on white's setup.

notes.explains: In the opening, both sides develop normally, so quick wins are rare. If the opponent makes odd moves, you gain time by developing and controlling the center.
notes.teaches: Play principled chess: develop pieces, fight for the center, and don't chase material at the cost of your position. Each wasted move by the opponent is a chance to improve your own setup.
notes.plans: Continue developing, castle, and then push in the center (like d5) to solidify your advantage.

notes.explains: In the Scotch opening, after Black takes the pawn, White should not recapture immediately because it helps Black develop. Instead, White should strike at the center, as Black has no pawn there.
notes.teaches: In open games, avoid trades that help your opponent develop. If your opponent has no central pawn, use your central pawns to gain space and initiative.
notes.plans: White should aim to build a strong center and develop pieces actively, while Black must be careful not to fall behind in development.

notes.explains: Moving the queen multiple times in the opening violates development principles. Here, the opponent's queen has moved too often, allowing the player to develop pieces with tempo and gain an advantage.
notes.teaches: In the opening, prioritize development and castle early. Avoid moving the same piece repeatedly, especially the queen, as it allows the opponent to gain time.
notes.plans: Continue developing pieces, castle, and prepare to punish the opponent's lack of development by creating threats.

notes.explains: After White plays Nf3, Black plays ...c6, which blocks the b8-knight's natural square and also stops the d-pawn from advancing. Black has now moved two flank pawns one square, completely sabotaging their own development. The engine already evaluates the position as clearly better for White.
notes.teaches: Flank pawn moves in the opening should have a clear purpose. Blocking your own knight's development is a serious mistake. Prioritize developing knights and bishops before moving pawns that don't help your center or piece activity.
notes.plans: White should continue developing with Nc3 or d3, and also consider taking the free pawn on e5. Black needs to find a way to develop pieces, but their position is already compromised.

notes.explains: Black plays ...g7-g7 (likely a typo for ...g6), which blocks the bishop on f8. This is a poor move because Black could have developed the bishop to c5, which would be active and not immediately attacked. Blocking your own pieces is a common beginner mistake.
notes.teaches: In the opening, develop your pieces to active squares. Avoid pawn moves that block your own bishop or knight. If you can develop a piece with tempo, do so.
notes.plans: Black should have played ...Bc5, developing the bishop and putting pressure on f2. Instead, ...g6 weakens the kingside and gives White time to consolidate.

notes.explains: White plays d3, which is a good move, activating the dark-squared bishop and preparing to develop the knight to c3 and castle. White is playing more naturally than Black, who has made several weakening pawn moves.
notes.teaches: A solid developing move like d3 can be strong because it opens lines for your bishop and supports the center. It's important to have a plan for development and king safety.
notes.plans: White should continue with Nc3 and castling, aiming to complete development and then use the initiative to attack Black's weakened kingside.

notes.explains: In this position, developing the bishop to c5 is natural, but the pawn structure can block your own pieces. White's d3 is a good move because it activates the dark-squared bishop and prepares knight c3 and castling.
notes.teaches: In the opening, prioritize development and king safety over grabbing pawns. A move like d3 can be strong because it supports the center and frees a piece.
notes.plans: White should continue with knight c3 and castling, aiming for rapid development.

notes.explains: Black has spent many early moves with the queen, leaving development far behind. The position is still playable, but Black must act decisively to avoid being overrun.
notes.teaches: In the opening, every queen move costs time; if you lag in development, you must create immediate threats or open the position before your opponent finishes mobilizing.
notes.plans: Black should look for active moves like f5 to challenge the center, but must be careful not to lock the center and allow White to develop freely.

notes.explains: Black's strategy of moving the queen repeatedly and blocking development leaves the rest of the army undeveloped, making the position strategically lost.
notes.teaches: In the opening, prioritize development over repetitive queen moves; a queen that moves often while other pieces stay home is a recipe for disaster.
notes.plans: White should continue developing and use the lead in development to launch an attack, while Black must try to catch up in development.

notes.explains: The opponent's setup resembles the Black Lion, but at a lower level, it's more practical to focus on sound development rather than trying to refute a specific system. The opponent's moves like ...Qb6 target the center, but White's pawns are adequately defended.
notes.teaches: Against unfamiliar or offbeat openings, prioritize natural development and castling. Don't overreact to threats that are not real; just continue with your plan.
notes.plans: Complete development by castling and bringing the other bishop out, then look for ways to challenge the opponent's setup.

notes.explains: Black has a developmental lead and should avoid unnecessary checks that don't improve the position. The bishop is well-placed on a solid square, and castling is a priority.
notes.teaches: At higher levels, avoid giving pointless checks that only help your opponent develop. Focus on sound development and king safety.
notes.plans: Castle kingside, develop the remaining bishop, and then consider central breaks or piece play.

notes.explains: In a position that is equal (0.1), black is slightly better due to faster development. The opponent's move queen f3 is a mistake because it leaves the knight undefended. The key is to notice that the knight is hanging, but only a meaningful attack matters—not a stupid one like queen b4 which gets defended.
notes.teaches: In the opening, development and king safety are paramount. When you see a hanging piece, ask 'then what?'—only attack it if you can do so meaningfully, not just to give a check or a simple attack that can be defended.
notes.plans: If the opponent makes a move that abandons a piece, look for a way to exploit it with a concrete sequence that wins material or creates a lasting advantage.

notes.explains: In the opening, after d3, the move Knight D5 is strong because it develops a piece, puts pressure on the opponent, and prepares to castle. It also prevents the opponent's freeing moves like Rook G8.
notes.teaches: In the opening, look for moves that develop with tempo and restrict the opponent's plans. A well-timed knight jump to a central outpost can be more effective than routine development.
notes.plans: If the opportunity arises, play Knight D5 immediately to seize the initiative. Follow up by attacking the opponent's weaknesses and preventing their counterplay.

notes.explains: In the second game, the opponent played d6 as black, which is fine, but then needed to continue with knight and bishop development. The speaker prefers more active center play but acknowledges the move is acceptable.
notes.teaches: After a passive first move, prioritize getting your knights and bishops out and preparing to castle. Fianchetto setups are okay but still require development.
notes.plans: Develop the knight to f6, fianchetto the bishop, and castle kingside.

notes.explains: In the opening, central pawns and pieces are key. Developing bishops to active squares can be risky if they can be chased by pawns, wasting time.
notes.teaches: Develop pieces with purpose, but be cautious about placing them where they can be attacked by pawns, forcing you to move again.
notes.plans: Develop the bishop to a safe square like b2, keep central pawns, and prepare to castle.

notes.explains: After castling, the opponent may castle opposite sides. This creates a race to attack, but here we choose to castle on the same side to connect rooks and simplify the position.
notes.teaches: Castling on the same side can lead to a quieter game where you can focus on piece activity and target weaknesses later.
notes.plans: Castle kingside, connect rooks, bring the queen out slightly, and prepare to trade pieces and exploit weaknesses.

notes.explains: In the Scandinavian, after developing the knight and bishop, you have the option to castle either side. Castling kingside is often faster and connects the rooks.
notes.teaches: Castle early to safeguard your king and connect your rooks. Choose the side that is faster and keeps your pieces coordinated.
notes.plans: After castling, focus on central pawn breaks and activating your bishop to increase pressure on the center.

notes.explains: When the opponent pushes pawns into your position, if you have developed and castled, you are well-prepared to defend. Here, the pawn push is met by taking the pawn, as it is not a real gambit like the Queen's Gambit.
notes.teaches: Recognize when a pawn offer is safe to take. Development and castling give you the resources to handle pawn advances.
notes.plans: Take the offered pawn, then be ready to trade pieces if the opponent attacks, maintaining the extra pawn.

notes.explains: The computer evaluates the position as plus two if White plays a specific sequence that includes retreating a piece, because it creates a long-term weakness in Black's pawn structure. White can then play h4, and if Black pushes g4, White can bring the knight back, forcing Black to advance pawns further, which weakens them.
notes.teaches: Sometimes it's worth spending time to provoke your opponent into creating permanent weaknesses, like overextended pawns. Pawns can't move backward, so they become long-term targets.
notes.plans: Play h4 to provoke g4, then use the knight to pressure the advanced pawns. Prepare breaks like f3 or maneuvers like Bc2 and Qd3 to create attacking chances.

notes.explains: Black plays b5, weakening their position and blocking their rook, giving the advantage back to white.
notes.teaches: Pawn moves can create permanent weaknesses; consider the long-term effects on your structure and piece activity.
notes.plans: Avoid weakening pawn moves unless they gain a concrete advantage.

notes.explains: A pawn move like a5 can destabilize the opponent's structure and hand the advantage back, because it weakens key squares and allows the opponent to start an attack.
notes.teaches: Every pawn move creates weaknesses; avoid moves that loosen your own structure without clear benefit.
notes.plans: If your opponent makes a weakening pawn move, look for ways to exploit the new weaknesses with your pieces.

notes.explains: When recapturing with a pawn, the choice of which pawn to use affects the pawn structure and piece activity. Taking with the f-pawn opens the bishop's diagonal and gives up control of c5, which can be beneficial if it activates pieces and creates attacking chances.
notes.teaches: When you have a choice of recaptures, consider the resulting pawn structure and which pieces get activated. Sometimes a structurally weaker recapture is better if it opens lines for your bishops and knights.
notes.plans: After recapturing with the f-pawn, aim to exploit the open diagonal for the bishop and continue the attack against the enemy king, possibly with moves like Qc2 or h4.

notes.explains: Pawns that have been pushed in front of the enemy king are called 'hooks' and can be used as targets for pawn advances to open lines against the king.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has advanced pawns in front of their king, use your own pawns to attack those hooks and force open files.
notes.plans: Aim to advance your pawns to challenge the opponent's pawns, creating open files for your rooks and queen.

notes.explains: Locking the position can neutralize an attack. If the pawns cannot get through, the attacker must find obscure sacrifices to break through.
notes.teaches: When facing a pawn storm, consider locking the pawn structure to block the attack. Centralize your pieces to support the blockade.
notes.plans: Place pawns and pieces to restrict the opponent's pawn advances, and coordinate your pieces in the center.

notes.explains: White later plays f4 again, but this time the pawn is an 'umbrella pawn'—it should not be attacking the king directly but rather creating structure. White also finds Qg1, a strong move, but black responds sharply with Qxd2+.
notes.teaches: Pawns should support the attack, not lead it. Also, always consider the opponent's checks and counterplay before committing to an attack.
notes.plans: White should use the pawns to control key squares and let the heavy pieces deliver the mate.

notes.explains: In closed positions, avoid creating weaknesses like having too many pawns on one color, which can give the opponent dominant control of key squares. Also, be wary of allowing enemy knights to occupy strong outposts like e5.
notes.teaches: Prevent the opponent from establishing dominant knights on central outposts by controlling those squares with pawns or pieces.
notes.plans: Consider moves that restrict the opponent's knight placement, such as advancing a pawn to cover the outpost.

notes.explains: Black defended well and got a reasonable position, leaving white with a damaged pawn structure (doubled pawns). White now wants to undouble and mobilize the pieces.
notes.teaches: When you have a damaged pawn structure, seek to repair it and activate your pieces. Against doubled pawns, the opponent should pressure the center, while the side with doubled pawns should aim to trade them off or use them dynamically.
notes.plans: Play to undouble the pawns and bring pieces to active squares, possibly with queen to a4 to create threats.

notes.explains: In the King's Indian, trading a bishop for a knight can damage the opponent's pawn structure. If the queen were on a square where it could recapture, the trade would be bad, but here the knight is pinned and cannot defend the center.
notes.teaches: Evaluate trades based on the resulting pawn structure and piece activity. A trade that damages the opponent's pawns is often good, even if it gives up a bishop for a knight.
notes.plans: After the trade, use the weakened pawn structure to your advantage, targeting the weak pawns and controlling the center.

notes.explains: White's attack is neutralized by taking a pawn with a pawn, preventing the pawn from advancing and opening lines. If the rook tries to line up, you can take the pawn and attack the rook.
notes.teaches: To stop a pawn storm, capture the advanced pawns; this can also open lines against the enemy pieces.
notes.plans: Keep the position closed if advantageous, and be ready to counterattack the enemy rook.

notes.explains: Avoid weakening your own position with unnecessary pawn moves, like b3, which can open lines for the opponent's pieces to infiltrate or give checks.
notes.teaches: Before making a pawn move, consider if it creates weaknesses; if a simple piece move achieves the same goal, prefer that.
notes.plans: Instead of weakening pawn moves, use piece moves to improve your position and maintain a solid structure.

notes.explains: In a position where black offers a trade of knights on d5, taking can be good because it undoubles pawns, but it also opens the light-squared bishop. The evaluation shows that taking is fine, but being too cautious allows black back into the game.
notes.teaches: When considering a capture, weigh the benefits (like fixing pawn structure) against the drawbacks (like opening lines for the opponent's pieces). Sometimes the best move is to take, but you must follow up actively.
notes.plans: After taking on d5, White should continue with active play, such as castling and preparing an attack, rather than playing passively.

notes.explains: The opponent gives away a bishop, and white can capture with either bishop or pawn. Taking with the pawn damages the structure, reminiscent of the Tartakower Caro-Kann, but taking with the bishop preserves structure.
notes.teaches: When capturing, consider the resulting pawn structure; avoid damaging your own structure unless there's a clear benefit.
notes.plans: Capture with the bishop to maintain a healthy pawn structure, then continue developing and preparing to attack the center.

notes.explains: White's pawn to c4 is a mistake because it weakens the center and allows black to lock down the center, leaving white's bishops blocked in. White should have developed the bishop instead.
notes.teaches: Pawn moves should support your center and piece activity, not just demonstrate you know how to move pawns. Develop pieces before making unnecessary pawn pushes.
notes.plans: White needs to find a way to free their bishops and create counterplay, while black should maintain the central blockade.

notes.explains: Recapturing with the f-pawn toward the center opens the rook's file and restricts the opponent's knight from developing to f3. This is a typical decision in such structures.
notes.teaches: When recapturing, consider which pawn move improves your piece activity and limits your opponent's options.
notes.plans: Use the open file for the rook and keep the opponent's pieces off key squares.

notes.explains: When the opponent plays c3 to prepare a central break and bring the knight back, the choice is between capturing and maintaining the pawn chain. Capturing is often better to avoid a damaged structure in the center.
notes.teaches: In pawn chains, avoid voluntarily creating a backward pawn or structural weakness; if the opponent offers a trade that resolves tension, consider taking to keep your structure sound.
notes.plans: After capturing, develop the knight to a central square, aiming to control key central files and diagonals.

notes.explains: After the queen trade, the pawn on f5 becomes less vulnerable, and kicking the knight with a pawn move is important because it removes the knight from its active post, preventing it from defending key squares like f6.
notes.teaches: Pawn moves can be used to drive away well-placed enemy pieces, especially when they are supporting the opponent's plans. Active defense means not allowing the opponent's pieces to settle.
notes.plans: Continue to activate pieces, put pressure on the e-file, and once the knight is driven back, the position should be favorable.

notes.explains: In a position where Black has doubled f-pawns after capturing a bishop, White can target the weak pawns and the exposed king. Doubled pawns are a structural weakness that can be exploited.
notes.teaches: Doubled pawns are a long-term weakness; aim to attack them and use open files.
notes.plans: Pressure the doubled pawns, keep the king safe, and prepare to castle.

notes.explains: After the opponent plays a poor move like Nh3, you can often punish it by exploiting the weakened pawn structure. Here, capturing on h3 with the bishop leads to doubled pawns for the opponent.
notes.teaches: When you can shatter the opponent's pawn structure, especially by doubling their pawns, it's usually a good deal—even if it means trading a bishop.
notes.plans: Recapture on h3 and continue developing, aiming to exploit the long-term weakness of the doubled pawns.

notes.explains: The defender emphasizes the importance of protecting all pawns, especially when they are potential passed pawns. If pawns are traded, the opponent's winning chances decrease, so keeping them protected is crucial.
notes.teaches: In endgame-like middlegames, pawn structure is vital; protect pawns to maintain winning chances and prevent the opponent from making progress.
notes.plans: Keep all pawns protected, and consider advancing pawns to create passed pawns or weaken the opponent's king.

notes.explains: Pawns work together and support each other. In this position, moves like c3 are weak because they don't contribute to the coordination of the pawns. The best response was to attack the pawn structure directly with a knight jump to d4.
notes.teaches: Always consider how pawns support each other; a pawn move that doesn't fit the structure can be a target. Use your pieces to attack such weaknesses.
notes.plans: Bring the rook into the attack and consider taking the pawn if it's undefended, as the resulting pressure can be overwhelming.

notes.explains: In double pawn structures, controlling light squares and playing f4 can be a key plan. Trading the bishop quickly and maneuvering the knight to e2 are part of a coherent setup.
notes.teaches: In closed or semi-open positions, focus on controlling key squares and improving piece placement with moves like f4 and Ne2.
notes.plans: Castle, then reroute the knight to e2, aiming for f4 and light-square control.

notes.explains: In a position where a pawn is attacked, defending it with another pawn is often the most effective because it creates a solid chain and makes it hard for the opponent to win the pawn back.
notes.teaches: When a pawn can be defended by another pawn, prefer that over piece defenses, as it strengthens your structure and reduces tactical threats.
notes.plans: Look for pawn moves that defend attacked pawns, maintaining a strong pawn chain.

notes.explains: In this position, neither side has clear weaknesses, and both are maneuvering. The player notes that a pawn move like f3 can block the opponent's bishop but also hinders their own development, highlighting the trade-off in such moves.
notes.teaches: When considering pawn moves, weigh the benefit of restricting the opponent's piece against the cost of weakening your own structure or blocking your development.
notes.plans: Look for ways to activate the dark-squared bishop, possibly with c5 or other breaks, while keeping an eye on the opponent's potential pawn breaks.

notes.explains: In this position, the opponent's queen is exposed on f3, and the pawn on e5 is vulnerable. Pushing the pawn to defend it would allow the knight to jump to e4, improving its activity and blocking our own knight's development.
notes.teaches: When your opponent attacks a pawn, consider whether defending it by pushing actually improves their pieces. Sometimes it's better to ignore the threat and find a more active continuation.
notes.plans: Instead of pushing the pawn, we can take the pawn with the queen or play a move like Bishop d6, forcing the queen to move and gaining time.

notes.explains: When you are up a pawn and have control of the position, there is no need to rush pawn moves that could open lines for the opponent. Moving pawns can create weaknesses and give the opponent counterplay.
notes.teaches: If you have a stable advantage, avoid pawn moves that don't contribute to your plan; instead, improve your pieces and maintain pressure.
notes.plans: Continue developing pieces and applying pressure on the queenside, e.g., with queen b6 and rook c8.

notes.explains: Pawns in front of your king are sensitive; advancing them can create weaknesses. Here, moving pawns like e5 could blunder the game, so it's better to keep them in place.
notes.teaches: Don't push pawns without a concrete reason, especially when they shield your king or control key squares. Piece play is often more valuable.
