notes.plans: White should capture the g5 pawn and then continue developing, while Black must address the hanging bishop.

notes.explains: A knight sacrifice on a7 can be devastating because it wrecks the king's position and wins back material, even if the king moves away.
notes.teaches: Always consider checks, even if they involve a sacrifice; a knight can jump over defenses and create chaos around the king.
notes.plans: If the opportunity arises, play knight to a7 check to shatter the king's safety and win material.

notes.explains: In a Queen's Gambit Accepted position, black's moves have left them completely lost. White has a tactical sequence involving a rook sacrifice to win a knight and bishop, leading to a decisive material advantage.
notes.teaches: Sometimes you must sacrifice material to gain a larger advantage. Here, giving up a rook for two pieces is a winning trade.
notes.plans: Execute the rook sacrifice, win the knight, then continue to win the queen, forcing resignation.

notes.explains: The computer suggests a deep sacrifice (f6, then bishop sacrifice, then rook sacrifice) to maintain dominance with the bishops, but the human player prefers a more practical approach.
notes.teaches: Computers often find spectacular sacrifices that are objectively best, but humans should weigh the risk and choose moves that are easier to handle over the board, even if slightly less optimal.
notes.plans: If not sacrificing, aim to keep the position closed and maintain the bishop pair, while gradually improving piece coordination.

notes.explains: A speculative sacrifice that is not based on concrete compensation is usually unsound. Here, the knight sacrifice fails because the follow-up check can be blocked, ending the attack.
notes.teaches: Before sacrificing material, verify that the resulting attack is real and cannot be easily parried. If the opponent can simply block or defend, the sacrifice is likely bad.

notes.explains: In a critical position, both bishops hang, and Black finds the best move Rook f2, giving up the knight with check. This allows the king to walk out to safety because the rook covers key squares. The move is hard to find but is the only way to keep the advantage.
notes.teaches: Sometimes you must sacrifice material to activate your king or to escape a pin. Look for checks that force the opponent's king to a worse square, even if it costs material.
notes.plans: Black should continue to harass the white king and coordinate the pieces to deliver mate or win more material.

notes.explains: Black spots a check and creates a fork, but white can handle it. White's c3 is the top engine move even though it loses a pawn, because white's massive development advantage means the attack will be devastating. The engine evaluates as plus seven, meaning black will have to sacrifice material to survive.
notes.teaches: Material is not always the most important factor. A huge lead in development and a vulnerable enemy king can justify sacrificing a pawn to open lines and accelerate the attack.
notes.plans: White should continue to open the center and bring all pieces into the attack, targeting the black king.

notes.explains: When a piece is attacked, sometimes it's better to sacrifice it for material if it's already won something, rather than trying to save it. Also, avoid useless checks that just move the king back without gaining anything.
notes.teaches: Don't play checks that don't accomplish anything; instead, improve your position. If a piece is trapped, consider sacrificing it for pawns if you've already gained material.
notes.plans: If the knight is attacked, either find a safe square or allow it to be captured if you've already won a bishop, gaining pawns in return.

notes.explains: A queen that has moved prematurely can become trapped. In this position, the queen on g3 has no safe squares because every potential move is covered by Black's pieces.
notes.teaches: Avoid bringing the queen out early unless there is a concrete threat; a developed queen can be a target. When your opponent's queen is exposed, look for ways to restrict its mobility.
notes.plans: Continue developing and attacking the trapped queen to win material.

notes.explains: A queen in the center of the board can be a target if it lacks escape squares. With pieces coordinating, you can trap the queen, winning material. Here, white uses pawns and pieces to restrict the queen's movement.
notes.teaches: A queen in the center needs many pieces to trap, but a knight only needs a pawn. Look for ways to limit the opponent's queen's mobility and create traps.
notes.plans: White plays Qf2 and Bf4 to take away queen squares, then advances pawns like g4 to further restrict, forcing black to sacrifice material to save the queen.

notes.explains: A queen among many enemy pieces can be trapped if it ventures too deep without support. In the game, Black's queen was lost due to a discovered attack, illustrating the danger of not checking piece protection.
notes.teaches: Always verify that the squares your pieces move to are safe, especially when attacking. A queen can be lost if it is surrounded by enemy pieces and lacks escape routes.
notes.plans: When ahead in material, consider giving up the queen for multiple pieces if it maintains a winning advantage, but avoid such losses when the game is balanced.

notes.explains: Players often spend time thinking after making mistakes, but it's better to think before committing to a move. Once a mistake is made, the position may already be lost.
notes.teaches: Invest your thinking time in the moves that matter—before you play them—not after. Recognize when a position is lost and focus on minimizing damage.

notes.explains: In this game, both players spent very little time on their moves despite having a long time control, leading to poor decisions.
notes.teaches: Time management is crucial; using your clock to think through positions is part of the game.

notes.explains: The opponent played g6 quickly and got mated in two moves. This shows the importance of not rushing moves and considering the opponent's threats.
notes.teaches: Always take time to check the opponent's possible checks, captures, and threats, especially when the position is sharp. Blitzing out moves can lead to immediate disaster.

notes.explains: In this position, black spent almost no time and got mated in two moves. The opponent had plenty of time on the clock but failed to check for immediate threats, leading to a quick loss.
notes.teaches: Always consider your opponent's possible checks, captures, and threats, even if they seem simple. Never assume your opponent will miss a tactic.

notes.explains: Time management is part of the game; playing well but running out of time still loses.
notes.teaches: Always save enough clock time; a good move is worthless if you flag.

notes.explains: The defender mentions that the clock is a piece, meaning time management is crucial in the game. They speed up moves to avoid losing on time, showing that practical considerations matter.
notes.teaches: Manage your clock as part of your strategy; avoid time trouble by playing efficiently, especially in complex positions.
notes.plans: Increase pace of play when necessary, and continue to seek active moves while maintaining solidity.

notes.explains: In a winning position with limited time, knowing the most efficient way to win is crucial. Even at lower ratings, players can learn to convert quickly.
notes.teaches: When you have a winning advantage, focus on the fastest, safest method to win, not just any winning move. Practice converting with a plan.

notes.explains: In this position, the opponent's queen is misplaced on the kingside, and the best way for White is to commit to the attack, otherwise the queen is just doing nothing.
notes.teaches: When your opponent leaves their queen out of play, you should either use it to create threats or accept that it is a liability and play accordingly.
notes.plans: Develop all pieces and castle, then deal with the consequences of the opponent's queen placement.

notes.explains: In this position, the queen capture is devastating because nothing is protected, unlike a previous game where everything was safe. The opponent's position is falling apart and they will lose material.
notes.teaches: When your opponent's pieces are unprotected, a queen incursion can be decisive. Compare with positions where the queen is safe and the attack fizzles.
notes.plans: Continue to exploit the unprotected pieces and convert the material advantage.

notes.explains: Against the Scholar's Mate attempt, Black can simply play h6 to prevent the bishop from pinning the knight, and then be ready to trade queens if needed, which removes mating threats.
notes.teaches: A simple move like h6 can neutralize early queen attacks, and trading queens is a reliable way to defuse an attack when you are not worse in the endgame.
notes.plans: Play h6, then if the queen trade happens, enter an endgame where Black has the bishop pair.

notes.explains: Scholar's mate attempts at higher levels are easily punished; here, Black wins material in just five moves because White's queen becomes overextended and the d4 pawn is weak.
notes.teaches: Do not rely on cheap traps; develop soundly and punish premature queen attacks by gaining time and attacking the queen.
notes.plans: After winning material, continue developing and convert the advantage without giving counterplay.

notes.explains: Black has a damaged pawn structure but has the bishop pair. The plan is to undouble the pawns and then use the bishops to exploit White's weaknesses, especially with the king still in the center.
notes.teaches: When you have the bishop pair, you should aim to open the position and target weaknesses, while also fixing your own pawn structure.
notes.plans: Play d6 and f5 to undouble the pawns, then use the bishops to pressure White's position.

notes.explains: In this position, White has the bishop pair and Black is underdeveloped, needing several moves to catch up. White can castle short and then break in the center, dominating with the bishops and rook. Black's long-term pawn weaknesses and poor piece coordination give White a lasting advantage.
notes.teaches: Recognize when your opponent makes a poor transformation, like trading pieces or moving pieces back without improving their position. Such moves can give the opponent a lasting advantage, especially if you have the bishop pair and better development.
notes.plans: Castle short, then break in the center to open lines for the bishops. Target Black's weak pawns and maintain pressure on the queenside.

notes.explains: After opening the enemy king, having the bishop pair and a dark-squared bishop can be decisive. Trading off the opponent's bishops reduces their defensive resources.
notes.teaches: In open positions with an exposed king, the bishop pair is a long-term asset; trade off the opponent's bishops to weaken their defense.
notes.plans: Use the bishops to control key diagonals, and consider moves like Nc5 to force trades or gain more attacking chances.

notes.explains: White's position has a space advantage and the bishop pair. Black's natural-looking move d5 is nearly losing because it opens lines for White's bishops and creates tactical threats.
notes.teaches: Be wary of pawn moves that open diagonals for your opponent's bishops. The side with the bishops wants open lines, so avoid blocking them or giving them targets.
notes.plans: White should look for ways to exploit the open diagonals, possibly with a Greek gift sacrifice on h7 if the opportunity arises.

notes.explains: White has a bishop pair and a long-range piece, giving them an advantage. The opponent's pawn structure is damaged, and white can start attacking the center.
notes.teaches: When you have the bishop pair, use your long-range pieces to pressure the center and avoid trading them off unnecessarily.
notes.plans: Develop the knight, castle, and then use pawns (like c5 and e-pawns) to chip away at the opponent's center, opening diagonals for the bishops.

notes.explains: White has the bishop pair but their diagonals are not easily opened. The plan is to get the queen and rooks into play, then use the e and c pawns to break apart the opponent's center.
notes.teaches: When you have the bishop pair, you need to open the position to give them scope; use pawn breaks to undermine the opponent's center.
notes.plans: Play b6, Bb7, and c5 to challenge the center, and bring rooks to central files.

notes.explains: When the opponent trades a bishop for a knight and then plays a pawn move like g6, the position remains comfortable for the side with the bishop pair, as long as development is completed and pressure is applied to weak pawns.
notes.teaches: The bishop pair is a long-term asset; after winning it, finish development and target the opponent's weaknesses rather than rushing.
notes.plans: Complete development and aim at the weak pawn, maintaining a comfortable advantage.

notes.explains: When facing a side with a strong bishop pair, the side with knights often wants to keep the position closed to limit the bishops' activity. Moves like f5 can restrict the knight and the center, though they may weaken the king's position.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, a pawn move that restricts the opponent's pieces can be worth a slight weakening of your own king's safety, especially if it helps neutralize the bishop pair.
notes.plans: Use pawn breaks like f5 and e4 to restrict the opponent's pieces and prepare to open the position only when it favors your own piece activity.

notes.explains: If the opponent plays passively, you have many good options; castling is natural, but trading off the bishop to get the bishop pair is also strong, especially for intermediate players.
notes.teaches: When the opponent does not pressure your center, take the opportunity to improve your position, either by castling for safety or by trading to secure the bishop pair.
notes.plans: Castle kingside to safeguard the king, or trade bishops to gain the two-bishop advantage.

notes.explains: White has a 'sniper bishop' on a2 (or similar diagonal) that exerts pressure along the long diagonal. The decision to trade or not trade pieces depends on keeping the bishop pair and maintaining pressure.
notes.teaches: Preserve bishops that are active on long diagonals; they can be powerful attacking pieces. When considering trades, evaluate whether you keep the bishop pair and whether the trade helps your opponent open lines.
notes.plans: If the opponent takes on d4, recapture and then play Nc6 to keep the bishop pair and maintain the sniper bishop's activity.

notes.explains: The player notes that the side with bishops generally wants to open the position, as bishops thrive in open space. They consider pawn breaks like h4, g3, or e5 to create open lines.
notes.teaches: When you have the bishop pair, aim to open the position to give your bishops long diagonals. Conversely, if you face the bishop pair, keep the position closed.
notes.plans: Look for pawn breaks that open lines for your bishops, but be wary of weakening your own king or pawn structure.

notes.explains: Black is building pressure on the e-file with rooks, and White is not blundering, so Black must find a way to make progress. Doubling rooks on the e-file is a good plan.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, doubling rooks on an open file is a standard way to increase pressure and create threats.
notes.plans: Play rook e7 and rook e8 to double rooks, then decide whether to trade rooks or win pawns.

notes.explains: With an extra bishop and a pawn advantage, the immediate priority is to trade rooks, simplifying to a won bishop-versus-no-bishop endgame. The move that threatens both winning more pawns and forcing the rook trade is especially strong.
notes.teaches: In endgames, simplifying when you have a material or piece advantage reduces the opponent's counterplay. Look for moves that combine threats, like attacking pawns while also offering a rook trade.
notes.plans: Trade rooks if possible, then use the bishop to defend the pawns and push them forward.

notes.explains: In a winning endgame, you don't need to overthink. Simple, effective moves are sufficient.
notes.teaches: When you are clearly winning, avoid complications and make straightforward moves that maintain your advantage.
notes.plans: Continue taking free pawns and simplifying, without burning time on complex calculations.

notes.explains: With a material advantage, the player wants to trade queens and rooks to reach a rook versus bishop endgame, which is winning.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, simplify the position by trading pieces, especially queens, to reduce counterplay and convert the win.
notes.plans: Trade queens and rooks, then use the extra material to win the endgame.

notes.explains: When you have a material advantage, it's often wise to simplify by trading pieces, especially rooks, to reduce the opponent's counterplay. In a dominant position, you can even run to the middle with your king, but generally, the corner is safer.
notes.teaches: In winning positions, trade pieces to eliminate any tactical tricks from the opponent. Use your material advantage to simplify and convert.
notes.plans: Trade rooks, then bring your queen forward, protect your pawns, and use your extra material to win the endgame. Avoid unnecessary risks by trading off the opponent's active pieces.

notes.explains: Black has a winning material advantage (two rooks vs rook and knight). The key is to simplify and then use the rooks to swarm White's pawns.
notes.teaches: In a winning endgame, simplify to reduce counterplay, then use your extra material to attack weaknesses.
notes.plans: Black attacks the pawn from behind, not from the front, to avoid the rook's protection.

notes.explains: In the endgame, black has a material advantage (extra rook) but white has counterplay. The engine suggests trading queens, but a human might play queen b3, leading to a drawish position. Black later has a chance to win but trades queens, restoring equality.
notes.teaches: When you are winning, simplify by trading pieces, especially queens, to reduce counterplay. Conversely, when defending, keep queens on to increase drawing chances.
notes.plans: If you are the side with the material advantage, aim to trade down to a winning endgame. If you are defending, create perpetual check or active counterplay.

notes.explains: In a winning endgame with extra pawns, simplifying by trading queens reduces the opponent's counterplay and makes your extra pawns more decisive, as rooks dominate without queens.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, aim to trade pieces, especially queens, to minimize risk and convert the win more safely.
notes.plans: Offer queen trades, activate rooks, and push passed pawns to create threats that force the opponent to defend passively.

notes.explains: Once the rooks are off, the position is trivially winning for the side with the extra bishop and pawns. The winning method is simple: keep the bishop protecting the pawns and advance them, avoiding any pawn losses.
notes.teaches: In a won endgame, the key is to avoid blunders that give back material. Keep pieces protecting each other and advance pawns in a coordinated way.
notes.plans: Move the bishop to defend the pawns, then push the pawns forward, ensuring they stay protected.

notes.explains: When the pawns are temporarily blocked, the king must join the action. The king can walk over to support the pawns and harass the enemy rook, while the opponent is reduced to passive defense or trying to create counterplay with their own passed pawn.
notes.teaches: In endgames, activate the king early. It is a powerful piece that can support pawns and attack enemy pieces. Do not rush; take time to improve your position.
notes.plans: Bring the king toward the center or the pawns, using it to kick away the enemy rook and support your own pawns.

notes.explains: In a pawn endgame with extra pawns, the active king is decisive. If the defender's pawns are gone, the attacking king can simply walk up and support the pawns, winning easily.
notes.teaches: In king and pawn endgames, king activity is paramount. With extra pawns, you should aim to use your king actively to support them.
notes.plans: Run the f-pawn forward, using the king to support it from behind or the side, while keeping the h-pawn as a reserve.

notes.explains: In an endgame, castling is often unnecessary; the king can safely move toward the center to participate in the fight.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, prioritize king activity over safety; the king becomes a strong attacking piece.
notes.plans: Move the king to a central square like d3 to support pawn advances and control key files.

notes.explains: White eventually finds the winning plan of running the king to c5 and b6, and later forces a queen trade to enter a winning endgame. The king becomes an active piece in the endgame.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, the king is a powerful piece. Use it actively to support pawns and attack the opponent's weaknesses.
notes.plans: Activate the king and force a queen trade to reach a winning endgame.

notes.explains: In the endgame, the king becomes a powerful piece, almost worth four points. We bring our king to the center to control key squares and support pawn advances.
notes.teaches: Activate your king in the endgame; it is a strong piece that should be centralized to control the board and assist in pawn promotion.
notes.plans: Bring the king to the center, then push pawns together, avoiding creating weaknesses, to create passed pawns and win.

notes.explains: The rook should be placed behind passed pawns, either to support their advance or to attack enemy pawns from behind. Giving pointless checks is a common mistake; only check when it serves a concrete purpose, like forcing the king to a worse square or winning material.
notes.teaches: Rooks belong behind passed pawns, both for defense and offense. Avoid random checks; every move should have a clear purpose.
notes.plans: Reposition the rook to its best square, either behind your pawns or to attack enemy pawns, and only give checks when they achieve something.

notes.explains: When pushing pawns to promotion, the king should escort them, and the rook should support from behind or the side. If the enemy king tries to block, use tactics like deflection checks to clear the way. Even if the bishop is given away, the extra pawns and active king are enough to win.
notes.teaches: In pawn races, escort the pawn with the king and use the rook to control key squares. Deflection checks can force the enemy king away from the promotion square. Material advantages like extra pawns and a more active king are decisive in king-and-pawn endgames.
notes.plans: Push the pawns with king support, use the rook to escort, and if necessary, sacrifice the bishop to promote. In king-and-pawn endgames, rely on the extra pawns and active king to win.

notes.explains: When defending against a single passed pawn, the king must be directly in front of the pawn. A side defense fails because the pawn can be pushed and the king cannot get back in time.
notes.teaches: The defending king must occupy a square in front of the passed pawn to stop it. Side defense is insufficient.
notes.plans: Push the pawn when the defending king is on the side, then use the king to shepherd it to promotion.

notes.explains: In a bishop endgame, Black wins not by checkmating but by pushing the g and h pawns. The bishop can dominate two pawns, but here one pawn can dominate two, which is why the opposition is important.
notes.teaches: In pawn endgames, the opposition is a key concept. A single pawn can hold two if it has the opposition.
notes.plans: Black should bring the bishop back and push the g and h pawns, using the king to support them.

notes.explains: Against an aggressive opponent who plays early queen moves, trading queens can lead to a favorable endgame or middlegame with a structural advantage.
notes.teaches: When facing early queen aggression, consider trading queens to neutralize the attack and transition to a position where your pieces are better placed.
notes.plans: If you have a lead in development or a safer king, offer a queen trade to simplify.

notes.explains: Trading queens early can be beneficial if it opens up the position and removes the opponent's right to castle. This can lead to a favorable endgame or middlegame.
notes.teaches: Don't shy away from early queen trades if they give you a positional advantage, such as weakening the opponent's king safety.
notes.plans: After the queen trade, continue developing and put pressure on weak pawns. Use the open files to activate your rooks.

notes.explains: The concept of continuity: each move affects the entire board, both your pieces and your opponent's. A single move can change the evaluation dramatically.
notes.teaches: Always consider how your move influences the rest of the position. Develop the skill of seeing the ripple effects of every move.

notes.explains: Continuity means understanding how the board changes after every move, even for pieces that don't move. A move can open lines or connect pieces, changing the tactical landscape.
notes.teaches: After each move, re-evaluate the entire board: what new threats, pins, or weaknesses appear? This prevents blunders like hanging mate in one.
notes.plans: Develop the habit of scanning the board after every move, especially for enemy threats to your king.

notes.explains: The concept of 'continuity' is crucial: players often forget that squares are protected or that pieces are en prise. In the game, a player played queen d4 thinking they won material, but the knight was protected and the queen was lost.
notes.teaches: Always check for piece protection and potential counterattacks before making a move. A tactic that seems to win material may fail if the target square is defended.
notes.plans: In positions where you are attacking, look for the opponent's defensive resources. If you are defending, look for ways to counterattack.

notes.explains: After Black plays ...f6 to challenge the center, White must respond by taking to maintain the pawn structure. Black recaptures with the rook, which is a reasonable move, but White then has a tactical opportunity to sacrifice a knight for two pawns, forcing g5 and opening lines against the king.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a knight sacrifice for two pawns is justified if it exposes the enemy king and creates lasting attacking chances. Evaluate such sacrifices based on the resulting initiative and king safety.
notes.plans: White should proceed with the sacrifice, aiming to open the g-file and bring the queen and rooks into the attack before Black can consolidate.

notes.explains: After the sacrifice, the position has rook and two pawns versus knight and bishop. The material balance is unclear, but the immediate priority is to use the exposed king to create threats.
notes.teaches: When you have sacrificed material for an attack, you must act quickly and concretely, as your lack of pieces means you cannot afford to let the opponent consolidate.
notes.plans: Play moves that force the king to move or create threats, such as queen checks or attacks on pawns, while preparing to bring the rooks into the attack.

notes.explains: In a position where the opponent has an extra pawn but has not castled, you can consider moves that prepare to win back material, like rook to b8, even if it temporarily loses a pawn, because you can recoup on b2. The board is big—there are counterplay opportunities.
notes.teaches: Don't be afraid to enter a pawn-down sequence if you have concrete compensation; look for tactical resources like winning back a pawn on the queenside.
notes.plans: Play rook to b8, allow the pawn to be taken, then take the b2 pawn with the bishop to restore material balance.

notes.explains: When defending against a queen with only pieces, the defender must minimize trades and keep as many pieces as possible to coordinate against the queen. Here, the material balance is rook, knight, and pawn for a queen, and the defender's pieces are active.
notes.teaches: Against a queen, avoid exchanging your pieces for the opponent's minor pieces or pawns. Keep your pieces coordinated to create threats and exploit the queen's awkwardness.
notes.plans: Coordinate the rook and knight to attack weaknesses and avoid trades, while defending the hanging pawn.

notes.explains: Trading a knight and bishop for a rook and pawn is unfavorable for the side giving up the two pieces, because two minor pieces generally outweigh a rook and pawn in the middlegame and endgame.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage of a piece, be willing to trade pieces to simplify into a winning endgame. Avoid giving up two pieces for a rook and pawn unless you have a clear compensation.
notes.plans: Continue trading pieces to reach a favorable endgame with the extra piece.

notes.explains: After a sequence like rook takes, bishop takes, king takes, the side with two pieces for a rook is better because the extra pieces are mobile and active, while the rook is stuck behind pawns and cannot easily enter the game.
notes.teaches: Two pieces are often worth more than a rook in the middlegame, especially when the pieces are active and the rook is passive.
notes.plans: With the extra pieces, centralize the king, push pawns, and develop the bishop to create four active pieces, while the opponent's rook remains trapped.

notes.explains: A prophylactic move like f4 can stop the opponent's intended plan forever. Here, f4 prevents Black from playing a move that would open the center, which would benefit Black because their king is exposed. White can then develop and castle safely.
notes.teaches: Prophylactic moves are important to anticipate and prevent your opponent's threats. By stopping their plan, you maintain control and avoid unnecessary complications.
notes.plans: Play f4 to solidify the center, then continue development and castle. If Black opens the center, use it to attack their exposed king.

notes.explains: When the opponent starts an attack on the flank, it's important to respond with prophylactic moves that address the threats. Here, advancing a pawn to h6 preemptively reduces the opponent's attacking potential.
notes.teaches: Use prophylactic thinking to anticipate and neutralize the opponent's attacking ideas before they fully develop.
notes.plans: Make solid defensive moves that also improve your position, such as advancing a pawn to limit the opponent's piece activity.

notes.explains: Black made a passive move like queen to c8, which doesn't improve their position. White, on the other hand, improved their position with every move, striking back on the side where the opponent expanded.
notes.teaches: Avoid passive moves that don't contribute to your plan. Instead, make every move improve your position, and counterattack on the side where your opponent is weakest.
notes.plans: Continue improving piece activity and prepare to open the center when your pieces are better coordinated.

notes.explains: After surviving the worst of the attack, you want to kick out the opponent's most annoying piece, such as a knight that has been causing trouble.
notes.teaches: When you have survived an attack, actively improve your position by removing or chasing away the opponent's active pieces.
notes.plans: Play a move that forces the annoying piece to move, then proceed to simplify the position.

notes.explains: In a sharp position, there are often multiple ways to handle the attack. Taking a pawn might be the best move but leads to a 'roller coaster ride,' while safer moves like h5 or trading pieces can avoid the attack but are less optimal.
notes.teaches: When facing an attack, you have choices: take the material and defend precisely, or make prophylactic moves to stop the attack. The best move is often the most forcing, but practical moves can be safer.
notes.plans: If you take the pawn, be ready to defend accurately. If you avoid the attack, you may need to play moves like h5 to stop the pawn storm, then break apart the opponent's pawns.

notes.explains: Black's ...e5 is a strong prophylactic move that immediately challenges White's center and opens lines for Black's pieces, giving them excellent play. White's position becomes uncomfortable because Black has more pieces in play.
notes.teaches: Prophylactic thinking involves anticipating your opponent's plans and taking measures to stop them. Here, Black prevents White's b5 and grabs central space, which is often more important than reacting to flank pawn moves.
notes.plans: Black should continue to develop and use the open lines to increase pressure, while White must find a way to consolidate and catch up in development.

notes.explains: White delays developing the kingside pieces to prevent Black's development. The move a6 is normal, and White should respond with a4 to stop ...b5.
notes.teaches: In Benoni structures, controlling the b5 square is crucial; a4 is a typical prophylactic move.
notes.plans: White continues with Qd2 and long castling, while Black may try ...Qb6 or ...Na6-b4.

notes.explains: The opponent is trying to create a solid, defensive wall, but the player believes it is 'pregnable' and that a breakthrough is inevitable.
notes.teaches: When your opponent is playing passively and defensively, it's important to remain patient and keep improving your position. Eventually, the defensive setup will crack under pressure.
notes.plans: Continue to improve piece activity, target weaknesses, and prepare to break through with a rook lift or pawn breaks.

notes.explains: The idea of 'playing tennis' in an even position means not rushing to force events. Instead, you make useful moves that improve your position and wait for the opponent to overextend or create weaknesses.
notes.teaches: In balanced positions, patience is a virtue. Make small improvements and avoid committing to irreversible pawn moves until the moment is right.
notes.plans: Continue to improve piece placement and maintain flexibility, looking for the moment when the opponent's position becomes vulnerable.

notes.explains: The move queen to d8 was not the computer's top choice (which was taking a pawn), but it was still good for Black. The idea was to shut down the opponent's ideas.
notes.teaches: Sometimes the best move is not the most materialistic but the one that prevents the opponent's counterplay. Prophylactic thinking—anticipating and stopping your opponent's plans—is crucial.
notes.plans: After queen to d8, Black maintains a solid advantage and can continue to improve the position, perhaps by activating the rook or preparing further advances.

notes.explains: When White has a strong initiative against Black's king, Black must anticipate White's attacking ideas, such as the maneuver Bh6 and Qg7, and find ways to neutralize them.
notes.teaches: Prophylactic thinking—predicting the opponent's plans and taking measures to stop them—is essential in sharp positions.
notes.plans: Look for moves that prevent White's key attacking resources, possibly by trading off dangerous pieces or creating counterplay.

notes.explains: The opponent's bishop move to g5 appears to have no clear plan after h6, suggesting it may be a hasty or misguided move. Black should be alert to such inaccuracies and continue improving while monitoring potential sacrifices on key squares.
notes.teaches: When the opponent makes a move without a clear threat, take advantage by improving your position and staying flexible. Always be aware of tactical motifs like sacrifices on squares near your king.
notes.plans: Continue with the queenside expansion and keep the knight well-placed, while being cautious about possible sacrifices on squares like g5 or h6.

notes.explains: When planning to long castle, you must anticipate the opponent's most forcing replies. Here, black can play Bg4, attacking the queen and disrupting white's plans. White must proactively prevent such ideas.
notes.teaches: When you have a plan, consider the opponent's best responses and prepare against them. Prophylactic thinking—preventing threats before they happen—is key to advancing.
notes.plans: White can play h3 to stop Bg4, or move the rook to a safer square, ensuring the king's safety before committing to long castling.

notes.explains: The opponent's move is unnecessary and weakens their position. Instead of avoiding trades, it's better to make progress with moves like knight to d4, anchoring it with c5.
notes.teaches: When you have a lead, make purposeful moves that increase your advantage; avoid unnecessary trades that help your opponent.
notes.plans: Play knight to d4, then support it with c5, maintaining pressure.

notes.explains: In a winning position, you can often choose between several good moves. Moves like a6 or b6 can be strong because they defend a pawn while also creating other benefits, such as attacking a rook or involving the queen.
notes.teaches: When you are winning, avoid rushing. Look for moves that improve your position while preventing your opponent's counterplay. Moves with tempo are often best.
notes.plans: Choose a move that defends the pawn and gains time, like b6, then continue to press your advantage.

notes.explains: The player is concerned about the opponent's pawns becoming powerful and considers anticipatory moves like preparing for the e-file opening. They also mention the possibility of trading pieces to simplify.
notes.teaches: Anticipate the opponent's pawn breaks and prepare responses, such as placing pieces to control key squares or being ready to recapture correctly.
notes.plans: Monitor the opponent's potential pawn advances and have a plan to neutralize them, either by trading, blocking, or counterattacking.

notes.explains: The queen on h5 attacks pawns and the rook, but the opponent can defend with g3. The queen also 'sees' the rook, which is annoying because it ties the rook down. The key is to keep creating one-move threats that force pawn advances, each one further exposing the king.
notes.teaches: In a mating attack, every pawn move by the defender is a concession that weakens the king's position. Keep poking at the king with small threats to force these pawn moves.
notes.plans: Continue to set up threats like queen h5, forcing the opponent to push pawns, then use the exposed squares to weave a mating net.

notes.explains: White must be careful not to lose the bishop on g5, as that would reduce the attack. Black has the resource rook g8, so White should consider prophylactic moves or be ready to respond accurately.
notes.teaches: In attacking positions, be aware of your opponent's defensive resources. Sometimes you must act decisively to maintain the attack, but also be willing to consolidate if needed.
notes.plans: Play knight f3, expecting the trade of bishops, and then continue with queen h6 or similar, keeping the initiative while being up material.

notes.explains: After Nxd3, White's rook on a2 is attacked, but taking it with Rxa2 would allow Rxb8, and Black's king would be stuck on the back rank with only one difficult defensive move. Thus, Nxd3 is a prophylactic move that removes the rook from the pin and avoids the tactical mess.
notes.teaches: Sometimes the best move is not the most materialistic one. Consider whether capturing a pawn exposes your king or pieces to a stronger counterattack. Defensive tactics are just as important as offensive ones.
notes.plans: After Nxd3, White can proceed with the plan of activating the rook and creating threats, while Black must find precise defensive moves to survive.

notes.explains: Snapping off a pawn can leave your king stuck on the back rank, under pressure. Here, the move that avoids that problem is knight takes d3, which is not just a trade but a prophylactic defensive move that enables rook takes a2.
notes.teaches: Before grabbing material, check if the capture exposes your king or allows the opponent to activate their pieces. Sometimes a defensive move that prevents counterplay is more valuable than winning a pawn.
notes.plans: After the prophylactic move, aim to play rook takes a2, forcing the white rook to a passive square. If the opponent has clearance to the last rank, consider moves like queen b2 to counter.

notes.explains: When the opponent plays a move like knight c5, it can be annoying because it attacks your pawns and creates threats. You need to respond accurately to maintain your advantage.
notes.teaches: In advantageous positions, be alert to the opponent's active moves. Sometimes a pawn move like a5 can prevent their ideas and secure your own.
notes.plans: Play a5 to stop b5, and if the opponent takes, you can recapture and still have winning chances due to your extra material.

notes.explains: After gaining material, it's tempting to chase the opponent's pieces, but it's often better to make patient improving moves, like bringing the rook into play or activating the bishop.
notes.teaches: Don't rush to attack without a follow-up; improve your position and wait for the right moment.
notes.plans: Improve piece activity and avoid pointless attacks that the opponent can easily meet.

notes.explains: With fewer pieces on the board, a queen becomes less powerful because it needs more pieces to support its activity. In this game, Black nearly equalized but needed to play more accurately. Eventually, Black hung a knight, and White won easily with rook domination.
notes.teaches: In endgames, the value of a queen decreases as pieces are traded. Keep pieces on the board if you have a queen, and trade pieces if you are defending against a queen. Also, always be alert for tactical blunders like hanging pieces.
notes.plans: In the endgame, use the rook to dominate open files and penetrate into the opponent's position. Convert material advantages by simplifying carefully.

notes.explains: In this position, the side with the knight and bishop against a rook and two pawns is better, even with the opponent's king exposed. The material imbalance favors the minor pieces because they coordinate well and the extra pawns are not enough compensation.
notes.teaches: When evaluating material trades, consider the activity and coordination of the pieces, not just the point count. A knight and bishop can be worth more than a rook and two pawns if they are well placed.
notes.plans: If you have the minor pieces, aim to keep the position closed and use the pieces to target weaknesses. If you have the rook, seek open files and pawn breaks to activate the rook.

notes.explains: In this position, after black's f5, the move g4 is a second-best option. It is aggressive but risky, as it weakens the kingside and can be met by counterplay. The alternative is to develop the bishop, which pins the knight and puts pressure on e4.
notes.teaches: When you have a pawn advanced, you have a choice between aggressive pawn pushes and sound development. The aggressive move may be tempting, but it must be carefully calculated; development is often more solid.
notes.plans: If you choose g4, be prepared to defend the kingside and use the space to launch an attack. If you develop the bishop, aim to increase pressure on the center and the pinned knight.

notes.explains: In an endgame with a material advantage, you should avoid unnecessary risks and one-move blunders. There are fewer pieces, so the margin for error is smaller, but the win is straightforward if you play solidly.
notes.teaches: In winning endgames, focus on safety and technique. Do not rush to attack; instead, improve your pieces, create passed pawns, and use your king actively.
notes.plans: Trade pieces when possible, advance your extra pawns, and centralize your king. Avoid pawn moves that create weaknesses.

notes.explains: In the endgame, black has extra material but wastes time taking all pawns and pushing unnecessary pawns. The key is to cut off the king and promote a pawn, not to grab every pawn or make extra queens.
notes.teaches: In winning endgames, focus on the most efficient path to checkmate or promotion. Don't overcomplicate; use your king and pieces to support a pawn's promotion.
notes.plans: Black should use the rook to cut off the enemy king, then push a pawn to promote, avoiding stalemate traps.

notes.explains: With a rook and six pawns against a knight and two pawns, the win is straightforward if you avoid unnecessary risks and keep pushing pawns.
notes.teaches: In a winning endgame, use your extra pawns to create passed pawns and force promotion; be relentless and precise.
notes.plans: Push the passed pawn, fork the king and knight, then promote to queen.

notes.explains: Many players at lower levels don't know what to do in the endgame because they only know how to attack for checkmate. Here the opponent kept trying to mate even though there was no mate, wasting time.
notes.teaches: When checkmating chances are gone, switch to endgame technique: be patient, manage the position, and use your material advantage.
notes.plans: Keep pushing the passed pawns and use the extra material to force a win.

notes.explains: As the game heads toward an endgame with an extra piece, it's often good to trade off bishops, especially the light-squared one, to further simplify and reduce any remaining attacking chances for the opponent.
notes.teaches: In a winning endgame, trade pieces to make the win easier. Avoid giving up two pieces for a rook and pawn, as that's usually not worth it.
notes.plans: Continue developing, castle, and then trade down to a winning endgame with the extra knight.

notes.explains: Against the Vienna or similar openings where the opponent tries to grab a pawn, the correct approach is to strike the center and not fear the pawn loss.
notes.teaches: Refute unsound gambits by centralizing and developing quickly; if the opponent takes a pawn, you can often regain it or get a lead in development.
notes.plans: Play natural developing moves, castle quickly, and maintain the extra pawn or compensate with activity.

notes.explains: In the reverse Vienna, Black's setup can be refuted by striking the center and then locking it, leading to a large advantage by move eight. The key is to understand the mechanics, such as the bishop to g5 pin.
notes.teaches: When facing a flexible or uncommitted setup, strike the center early and be ready to exploit the resulting pawn structure. Understanding the typical tactical motifs in an opening helps refute it.
notes.plans: Continue developing while maintaining the central pawn duo, and look to expand further with e5 if Black does not address the center.

notes.explains: Against a 'hippo' setup where Black avoids committing, White can build a massive center with four pawns. The immediate threat is to push e5, forcing Black's knight to move to an awkward square.
notes.teaches: When your opponent plays passively, maximize your central pawn presence. A pawn push like e5 can cramp the opponent and create tactical opportunities if their pieces are poorly placed.
notes.plans: Prepare e5, and if Black's knight goes to h5 or g4, trap it with pawn moves like h3. If Black plays Ne4, be ready to challenge it.

notes.explains: After the center is locked and Black's pieces are poorly coordinated, White can launch a direct attack. Even if Black tries tricks like Bxf3 and Qh4+, the king can sidestep to e2 and f1, and Black's pieces remain trapped.
notes.teaches: When you have a large material or positional advantage, you can often ignore normal principles like castling. Look for forcing moves that maintain the initiative and keep the opponent's pieces offside.
notes.plans: Continue the attack by pushing h4 and g4 to open lines against the enemy king. Use the material advantage to justify pawn sacrifices that expose the king.

notes.explains: After the attack fizzles, the opponent's rook on b1 targets the b7 pawn, and the natural follow-up is to push f3 to open lines against the king. White instead played a passive move, missing the chance to create threats.
notes.teaches: When you have a lead in development or an attack, keep the pressure on by opening lines and creating threats; don't let the opponent regroup.
notes.plans: White should play f3 to open the f-file and continue the attack; black must defend carefully.

notes.explains: In this attacking position, Black has several defensive resources like ...f6 and ...h6, so the attack is not immediately decisive. White's pieces are active, and the position offers good attacking chances.
notes.teaches: When you have an attack, consider prophylactic moves that prevent the opponent's defensive resources, and be willing to build up slowly rather than forcing immediate wins.
notes.plans: Continue developing and preparing the attack, possibly with moves like Qc2 to support a future sacrifice or to accelerate castling.

notes.explains: White chose to leave the king in the center and attack Black's castled king, demonstrating that castling is not always necessary for an attack. The attack succeeded because Black's pieces were poorly placed to defend.
notes.teaches: You can launch a kingside attack without castling, especially if the opponent's king is exposed and your pieces are active. Central king safety can be acceptable if you have the initiative.
notes.plans: White aimed to open lines and bring pieces like the queen and knight into the attack, threatening mate on the light squares.

notes.explains: In a position where the opponent's pieces are tied down, you can often sacrifice material to rip open lines against the king. The attack is justified because the opponent's pieces are not coordinated to defend, and the king remains vulnerable.
notes.teaches: When you have a lead in development or the opponent's king is exposed, consider dynamic sacrifices to open lines. The key is to ensure that the attack is unstoppable, even if material is traded off, because the final mating net is decisive.
notes.plans: Continue to bring your heavy pieces to the open files and aim for a mating attack, using sacrifices if necessary to remove defenders or open the king's position.

notes.explains: Black's attack continues with moves like Qg5, threatening to capture on g2 and keep the white king trapped. Even if material is down, the positional bind on the king makes white's position miserable.
notes.teaches: In attacking positions, keep the opponent's king in the center and avoid allowing them to castle. Use threats to maintain pressure and prevent consolidation.
notes.plans: Continue the attack with Qg5, aiming to create threats against g2 and the king.

notes.explains: When attacking the king, it's often better to start with a rook rather than the queen, because the rook is less valuable. The queen can be brought in later to deliver the final blow.
notes.teaches: Lead an attack with a rook to avoid exposing your queen. Bring the queen in later when the attack is more developed.
notes.plans: Look for rook checks or rook lifts to start the attack, then bring the queen to support.

notes.explains: In the resulting position, White can slowly build up by developing the bishop, targeting the pawn, and bringing the rook to open files. The black king is exposed, and a knight to g5 with queen support can create a decisive attack, culminating in a bishop h7 sacrifice leading to double check and winning the queen.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed and pieces are coordinated, a sacrificial attack can be decisive. Look for patterns like bishop sacrifices on h7 and double checks.
notes.plans: White should continue to bring pieces to the attack, aiming for a mating net, possibly with queen to d6 mate.

notes.explains: White plays e4, which accomplishes nothing, and Black responds with g5, attacking the knight. White then finds the best move of the game: Qh5, exploiting the weak king. Black's king is forced to step out, and White's rook comes to d1, showing that even down material, the attack is strong.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed, every tempo counts. A queen sortie like Qh5 can create immediate threats, and bringing the rook to the open file intensifies the pressure. Material is secondary to a winning attack.
notes.plans: White should continue the attack, using the queen and rook to create threats against the black king. Black must defend accurately and try to consolidate the material advantage.

notes.explains: With queens and kings facing each other on an open board, White should open the center to exploit the black king's exposure. Trading queens would be a mistake because White needs the queen for the attack.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is vulnerable and you have a development lead, avoid queen trades and open lines to bring all your pieces into the attack.
notes.plans: White should push forward with pawn breaks and piece play, aiming to create an avalanche of attackers against the black king.

notes.explains: White has a material advantage and active pieces, and Black's king is exposed due to the early f6 move. White's attack is overwhelming.
notes.teaches: When you have a lead in development and material, look for ways to bring all your pieces into the attack, especially the rooks, and target the opponent's weak king.
notes.plans: White should continue the attack, bringing the rook to the open file and using the queen to deliver threats, while Black must try to defend and block checks.

notes.explains: In this position, the opponent's king is exposed and has been forced to push pawns in front of it. The attacking side has a material or positional advantage and is threatening mate. The key is to maintain the initiative and avoid unnecessary checks that could allow the defender to consolidate.
notes.teaches: When you have a winning attack, focus on the most forcing and aggressive moves that maintain the threat of mate, rather than taking time to grab material. Forcing the opponent to weaken their king's pawn shield is often decisive.
notes.plans: Continue the attack by bringing more pieces to bear on the king, using the queen and knights to create mating threats. If the opponent tries to defend, look for tactical blows that remove key defenders.

notes.explains: After winning material, the focus should shift to attacking the king. The knight is protected and can jump to e6, attacking many valuable pieces, while the rook pressures along the line.
notes.teaches: When you are up material, coordinate your pieces to target the enemy king. Look for outposts like e6 for knights that can create multiple threats.
notes.plans: Use the knight to jump into e6, supported by the rook, to attack the king and win more material. Alternatively, consider queen h6 with rook support to break through.

notes.explains: After the king is opened, the attacker must be alert to counterplay. The opponent's queen move was not a real threat, so the pawn push was safe and the rook lift to the seventh rank becomes decisive.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage and an exposed enemy king, use your active pieces to create direct threats, but always check whether the opponent's replies are genuine threats or just noise.
notes.plans: Continue pushing the g-pawn and aim for rook h8, followed by queen h7, to force mate or win material.

notes.explains: In a winning attack, the king is corralled like a shepherd dog; the goal is to restrict its escape squares rather than chase it wildly. Here, a controlled check like queen f5 forces the king to the back rank, and as long as the king cannot run forward, checkmate follows within a few moves.
notes.teaches: When attacking a king, prioritize controlling its escape squares over giving flashy checks. A calm, restricting move is often more effective than a series of checks that allow the king to flee.
notes.plans: Continue to cut off the king's escape, bring the rooks into the attack, and deliver mate without allowing the king to advance.

notes.explains: When the opponent's king is exposed, the queen alone is insufficient to deliver mate; it needs support from other pieces. Here, the queen's attacks are easily parried because the rook can simply move to safety.
notes.teaches: To offset a material deficit, you must hunt the enemy king with coordinated pieces, not just one. A lone queen's threats are not enough.
notes.plans: Bring additional pieces into the attack, such as a knight to c7, to create real mating threats.

notes.explains: White runs with the king, and black gives many checks, but the king escapes. The speaker notes that giving a million checks is useless if you run out of pieces.
notes.teaches: When your opponent's king is fleeing, don't just give checks without a plan. Coordinate your pieces to cut off escape squares or bring in reinforcements.

notes.explains: Black plays Bg7, but White's rook to d1 and queen to g4 create devastating threats on the light squares. Black's king is forced to run forward, and White's queen re-enters the game with Qa5, but Black misses the best defense and loses material.
notes.teaches: In a king hunt, the defender must find precise moves to survive. When your king is exposed, you must be willing to give back material to stop the attack. Conversely, the attacker should keep the initiative and not allow the defender to consolidate.
notes.plans: White should continue to press the attack, while Black must try to coordinate the pieces and find a way to neutralize the threats.

notes.explains: In this Dutch Defense setup, pinning the knight and capturing it damages White's pawn structure, which is a recurring theme. There is a known trap involving a5, a3, a4, Qb4, Nc6, Qb5, and Ra5 that traps the queen, but it only works if the opponent cooperates.
notes.teaches: Pinning and capturing a knight to ruin the opponent's pawns is a standard structural gain. Be aware of tactical traps in the opening, but don't force them if the opponent can avoid them.
notes.plans: Develop naturally, castle, and prepare to place the bishop on the long diagonal (b7) to pressure the center.

notes.explains: The Dutch Defense gives Black a comfortable position with a pawn on f5, which anchors a knight on e4 and provides a transfer point through f6. This setup is easy to play and often leads to opponent mistakes like a3 or a4.
notes.teaches: The Dutch Defense is a practical opening at club level because it creates a solid structure and clear plans. The f5 pawn supports a knight on e4 and gives Black active play.
notes.plans: Develop pieces harmoniously, aim to plant a knight on e4, and be alert to typical opponent inaccuracies like a3/a4, which can be punished.

notes.explains: Against the London System, the Dutch setup with ...Nf6 and ...Bb7 is still playable, but the London's early c3 prevents the typical ...Bb4 pin, so the bishop must go to e7 or d6 instead.
notes.teaches: When your preferred setup is disrupted by the opponent's move order, adapt by choosing an alternative square for the piece that still fits your plan.
notes.plans: Develop the bishop to e7 or d6, castle, and prepare a central break with ...Qe7 and ...e5.

notes.explains: Against the Dutch Defense, the Staunton Gambit (e4) is an aggressive try. It's possible because of the specific pawn structure, but the excerpt doesn't provide the exact continuation.
notes.teaches: In the opening, be aware of gambits that challenge your setup. They can be dangerous if you don't know the correct response.
notes.plans: If facing the Staunton Gambit, consider how to maintain the pawn or return it for development and activity.

notes.explains: In the Dutch Defense, the Stonewall setup creates a solid pawn structure on light squares, but the light-squared bishop is often problematic. Development must account for the opponent's potential to block key moves.
notes.teaches: In the Stonewall Dutch, develop the light-squared bishop actively, often to d7 or e6, and be aware of pawn breaks like e5 or f5 to open the position.
notes.plans: Develop pieces, castle, and prepare to attack on the kingside or in the center depending on where the opponent castles.

notes.explains: After developing the bishop to b7, the plan is to plant a knight on e4 and later jump to f6, supporting a kingside attack. The h-pawn can serve as a hook to open lines, and moves like Qh4 bring the queen into the attack.
notes.teaches: Centralized knights on e4/f6 can coordinate with a queen on h4 and a rook to build a kingside initiative. A pawn on g4 can be a lever to open the h-file.
notes.plans: Play Nbd7, Nf6, Qh4, and prepare g5-g4 to open lines against the enemy king.

notes.explains: In a tactical sequence, after a series of captures, the position offers a chance to play a desperado: instead of recapturing, sacrifice the knight to hit the queen, gaining material in the long run. This leads to an extra pawn and a strong passed pawn on d5.
notes.teaches: A desperado is a forcing move that extracts maximum value from a piece that is doomed anyway. Always look for intermediate checks or threats before recapturing.
notes.plans: After winning the pawn, expect d5 to open the bishop's diagonal, and consider pushing e5 to gain space.

notes.explains: In this position, White's knight on f7 is attacked, but instead of retreating, White can play Nxf7, a desperado move. This sacrifices the knight but hits the queen and gains time, making the loss on White's terms.
notes.teaches: A desperado is a tactic where you use a piece that is doomed anyway to create maximum damage before it falls. Look for forcing moves that give you compensation.
notes.plans: White should play Nxf7, attacking the queen, and then follow up with moves that exploit the weakened black kingside.

notes.explains: When your queen is hanging, you can sometimes use a desperado tactic: instead of saving it, you take as much material as possible before the queen is captured, often with checks.
notes.teaches: In a losing or equal position, look for desperado sequences where you trade your queen for maximum compensation, especially if you can give checks along the way.
notes.plans: Calculate capture sequences that maximize material gain before the queen falls, and consider checks to force the opponent's responses.

notes.explains: With the bishop on an open diagonal, a move like Qc4 can create a double attack, threatening to win the queen if the bishop is captured. This is a critical resource that turns the game decisively.
notes.teaches: When a bishop has a clear diagonal, look for queen moves that exploit pins or skewers to win material. Always check for such tactical shots before settling for a quiet move.
notes.plans: Play Qc4, and if the opponent plays b3, offer a queen trade to simplify into a winning endgame.

notes.explains: A quiet move like Qc1 can be very strong because it hits multiple targets at once, but it is hard to see. Instead, a more natural move like Rb1 may be less effective.
notes.teaches: Look for moves that create multiple threats simultaneously; they are often the strongest but require careful calculation.
notes.plans: When attacking, consider centralizing the queen or doubling rooks to increase pressure.

notes.explains: Black's queen to d4 is a strong move because it attacks two pieces at once (the bishop on c4 and the pawn on e4). White must find a way to defend both, which is difficult.
notes.teaches: When you can create a double attack, do it. The opponent is forced to deal with multiple threats, and if they can't, they lose material.
notes.plans: White should look for a move that defends both attacked pieces, such as queen to e2, but if that's not possible, they may have to give up something.

notes.explains: When two rooks are hanging and the piece between them cannot move, it's a brutal coincidence that allows attacking both rooks simultaneously.
notes.teaches: Always be aware of hanging pieces and look for double attacks, especially when the opponent's pieces are undefended and constrained.
notes.plans: Capture the hanging material and convert the advantage.

notes.explains: A move like bishop to e2 may seem quiet, but it sets up multiple threats, such as queen to g5 or queen to h1, which can win material or create mating threats. The opponent is forced to deal with these ideas, often losing material.
notes.teaches: Look for moves that create multiple threats or zugzwang-like pressure. A single move that attacks a piece while also threatening a decisive tactic can be very powerful.
notes.plans: When you have a material advantage, use threats to force the opponent into passivity, then improve your position and convert the advantage.

notes.explains: A move like bishop to h6 can serve a dual purpose: it attacks the rook and also threatens mate, forcing the opponent to respond with a specific defensive move that may weaken their position.
notes.teaches: Look for moves that create multiple threats simultaneously; the opponent may be forced to address the most dangerous one, allowing you to gain material or positional advantages.
notes.plans: After the opponent's forced response, continue to press the attack, using the coordination of your pieces to maintain the initiative.

notes.explains: A move that attacks a rook might also open an attack on a bishop. Beginners often miss such double attacks because they focus on the most obvious threat.
notes.teaches: Always look at all your pieces and the side effects of each move. A single move can create multiple threats.
notes.plans: Look for moves that create multiple threats, like a pawn move that attacks a rook while opening a line for your queen to attack a bishop.

notes.explains: The position is tactically sharp: a capture would allow bishop f6, winning the queen, so the immediate recapture is not safe. The queen on c4 creates major problems for the opponent, and the player is confident of an advantage.
notes.teaches: Always check for tactical resources like bishop f6 before recapturing; a seemingly natural capture can be a blunder if it hangs the queen.
notes.plans: Consider moves that solve multiple problems at once, such as knight e4, which addresses both the bishop f6 threat and the recapture.

notes.explains: After an exchange on e4, it's tempting to recapture automatically, but here White has a strong resource: bishop f6, which would give White active play in Black's territory. Black must spot this and choose a different move to shut down White's activity.
notes.teaches: Always check for tactical resources before recapturing. Sometimes the automatic recapture allows the opponent to seize the initiative; look for a move that maintains your advantage.
notes.plans: Find a move that neutralizes White's counterplay, such as a move that prevents bishop f6 or creates a threat of your own. Stay methodical and avoid complacency.

notes.explains: Black played queen h5, which threatens a mate but actually hangs mate in two. The speaker loves the move because it shows the player knows what to look for (checkmate threats), even though it's tactically flawed.
notes.teaches: Even if a move is not objectively best, it can be instructive if it shows a good idea. Always look for checks and threats, but also calculate your opponent's replies.

notes.explains: The position is sharp and the opponent is playing very quickly, which pressures the speaker to keep pace. The speaker is monitoring potential sacrifices on a specific square and is cautious about a clumsily placed knight.
notes.teaches: When facing a fast opponent, stay alert to tactical threats like sacrifices, and be willing to reposition clumsy pieces even if it costs a tempo.
notes.plans: Continue developing harmoniously, improve the knight's placement, and avoid creating weaknesses while preparing to expand on the queenside.

notes.explains: In this position, the opponent must remember that a defensive move like rook f1 leaves their own pawn weakened. The key is to spot tactical resources like rook a7 that exploit such weaknesses immediately.
notes.teaches: Always be alert to the consequences of defensive moves; they can create new weaknesses. Look for immediate tactical shots that punish the opponent's inattention.
notes.plans: Continue to apply pressure by targeting weakened pawns and using active rook placement to create threats.

notes.explains: After the opponent's bishop move and knight to g5, the position becomes bad for the side whose queen is attacked. The queen must move, and if the opponent forks, it can lead to checkmate or a triple fork, making the position losing.
notes.teaches: Always spot tactics for your opponent before making a move. Avoid autopilot moves; check if your queen or other pieces can be attacked.
notes.plans: If your queen is attacked, find a safe square that avoids forks and maintains your position. Consider backward moves if they are safe and useful.

notes.explains: The knight on e4 is strong because it dominates the opponent's bishop, which is useless on dark squares while the light squares are of different quality. The player is up two pawns and can simplify to a winning endgame.
notes.teaches: A well-placed knight can outpost a bishop, especially when the bishop is limited by its own pawn structure. Use piece activity to convert a material advantage.
notes.plans: Trade pieces to reach a knight or rook endgame, using the extra pawns to win. Keep the position closed to prevent counterplay.

notes.explains: With a two-pawn advantage, the player plans to trade queens and simplify to a rook endgame, which is a straightforward win. They keep the rook active and centralized, and bring the king up to support the pawns.
notes.teaches: In a winning endgame, trade pieces to reduce counterplay, keep your rook active, and bring your king to support passed pawns. Always be ready to defend your pawns.
notes.plans: Trade queens, then bring the king to the center, push the passed pawns, and use the rook to protect them while advancing.

notes.explains: In a Dutch Defense position, Black has a choice between queen h4 and queen g5. Queen g5 is particularly strong because it forks the queen and mate threats, but queen h4 is also good. The position plays itself after d6 and knight d7.
notes.teaches: When you have multiple good moves, choose the one that creates the most threats. Look for moves that combine attacking ideas, like forking the queen and mate.
notes.plans: Develop the queen to an active square, then continue with natural moves like d6 and knight d7, maintaining pressure on the kingside.

notes.explains: In a race to attack, your queen can often get to the defense faster than the opponent's pawns can advance. Here, the queen was able to defend the weak pawn.
notes.teaches: When facing a pawn storm, consider using your queen to defend key squares, as it can move quickly.
notes.plans: Bring the queen to defend critical points and then counterattack.

notes.explains: After e3 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4, Black plays …e4, and White responds with Nd2. White's position is already better because Black's pawn on e4 is overextended and can be undermined.
notes.teaches: When your opponent has a big pawn center, look to undermine it with pawn breaks like c4, and then target the pawns with pieces like Nc3 and Qb3.
notes.plans: White should play c4, then Nc3, and possibly Qb3 to pressure the e4 pawn.

notes.explains: Black plays Qf6, a vague move that doesn't have a clear purpose. The engine evaluates it as bad, giving White a plus two. Moving the queen out early without a plan can be a mistake.
notes.teaches: Don't bring your queen out early without a concrete plan. It can become a target and neglect development.
notes.plans: Black should focus on developing pieces and castling, rather than moving the queen aimlessly.

notes.explains: White, who had not used pawns earlier, now creates pawn breaks to soften the center and open lines for pieces.
notes.teaches: Pawn breaks are essential to activate pieces and create play; don't neglect your pawns.
notes.plans: Continue using pawn breaks to open the position and bring pieces into the attack.

notes.explains: Black has a chance to play d5, a tempo-winning move that attacks the bishop and gains space in the center. This would force White's bishop to move again, further delaying White's development.
notes.teaches: Use pawn breaks like d5 to gain space and create threats that force your opponent to react, especially when they have undeveloped pieces.
notes.plans: Black should play d5 to challenge the center and continue developing.

notes.explains: We need to maintain tension and avoid overextending. Moves like c4 can be risky because they open lines for the opponent, but they also open the c-file for us.
notes.teaches: In complex middlegames, weigh the risks and benefits of pawn breaks; sometimes maintaining tension is better than committing.
notes.plans: Keep the tension, see how black responds, and be ready to exploit any weaknesses.

notes.explains: After black plays Rf8, white should consider trading rooks or maintaining tension on the f-file, but instead avoids trades and gives up the file, allowing black to double rooks and attack the king.
notes.teaches: When you are winning, trading pieces is often good, but don't surrender an open file; keep control of key files.
notes.plans: Play Qd2 or Qe2 to keep the rook tension and control the f-file.

notes.explains: White plays h3 on the side where black is attacking, creating a target for black to later open the h-file and attack the king.
notes.teaches: Avoid creating pawn weaknesses on the side where you are under attack; instead, trade pieces or defend actively.
notes.plans: Consider trading pieces to reduce the attack, rather than making weakening pawn moves.

notes.explains: White plays a passive move Ra1, losing a knight for no compensation, when there were active options like trading rooks or breaking open the center.
notes.teaches: In active positions, look for forcing moves and avoid passive retreats that give up material for nothing.
notes.plans: Seek active continuations: trade rooks, open the center, or create threats.

notes.explains: A piece can be sacrificed not for an immediate attack but because the engine sees a deep follow-up that a human will never find in practice. Here White loses a knight for no visible compensation, and the engine's line (Rc1, d5, Qd4) is unrealistic.
notes.teaches: Do not rely on engine-only sacrifices in practical play; if you sacrifice material, make sure you have a concrete, humanly findable plan to justify it.
notes.plans: If you have sacrificed material, look for ways to open lines against the king or create immediate threats; otherwise, the sacrifice is just a blunder.

notes.explains: In a critical position, the defender must find the only move to stay alive. Here, Qe5 was necessary, but Qf6 allowed a decisive combination involving Qd5, Qa8, and a rook lift.
notes.teaches: When defending, look for the move that covers all threats; often the best defense is a counterattack or a move that creates escape squares.
notes.plans: If you are the attacker, look for combinations that exploit the opponent's inability to find the only move.

notes.explains: A bishop move like Bc6 can blunder a mate because it abandons a key square (g2) that the queen needs to cover. The opponent then has a forced mate with Qf2 and Rg3.
notes.teaches: When moving a piece, check which squares you are leaving undefended; a single move can open the door to a mating net.
notes.plans: If you see a potential mate, calculate all forcing moves, including checks and captures, to confirm it.

notes.explains: In this attacking position, the queen is more valuable than a free rook because it can participate in a mating attack. The opponent gives check, but the defender has a forced mate in two with rook and queen.
notes.teaches: When attacking, prioritize bringing your most powerful pieces (queen and rooks) to the attack, even if it means declining material gains.
notes.plans: Execute the mating pattern: check the king, bring the rook to the third rank, and deliver mate with the queen.

notes.explains: In a winning position, the king is stuck in the center and the opponent's pieces are hanging. The winning idea involves bringing a bishop along a diagonal to deliver check and eventually mate, but it's hard to see because of the empty squares.
notes.teaches: Visualize the squares your pieces control as 'spots' or 'arrows' to see how they restrict the enemy king. This helps spot mating nets.
notes.plans: When the enemy king is in the center, use your pieces to control escape squares and bring more force to the attack.

notes.explains: In a winning position with many mating threats, it's important to find the quickest mate; here, several queen moves were mate in one or two, but a rook move was not mate because the rook could be captured.
notes.teaches: When you have a decisive attack, look for forcing moves like checks and mates, and avoid moves that allow the opponent to defend.

notes.explains: A rook can follow a path to a square like c6 where it attacks both the queen and the king, creating a decisive double attack. This turns a losing position into a winning one.
notes.teaches: Rooks are powerful on open files and can often deliver decisive forks when they penetrate the opponent's position.
notes.plans: When your rook is active, look for squares where it can attack multiple high-value pieces simultaneously.

notes.explains: When the opponent's king is exposed, perpetual check can be a saving resource. Here, Qd5 gives perpetual check, turning a losing game into a draw.
notes.teaches: In a losing position, look for perpetual check patterns to salvage a draw.
notes.plans: If you are winning, avoid allowing perpetual check by keeping your king safe or blocking checks.

notes.explains: A simple move like Rf1 attacking a bishop can be a fork if the bishop is also protecting a promotion square. Here, a4 blunders a fork and a promotion.
notes.teaches: Always check if your opponent's pieces are overloaded; a simple attack can turn into a decisive fork.
notes.plans: When you see an undefended piece, look for ways to attack it while also creating a second threat.

notes.explains: In a position with tactical opportunities, you can set up a fork or a sacrifice to win material. Here, knight to f4 threatens knight to d3, a fork, and if the opponent doesn't address it, you can sacrifice a knight to replace it with another, leading to winning the queen.
notes.teaches: Look for tactical patterns from a distance, such as forks and sacrifices, and set up threats that force the opponent to respond or lose material.
notes.plans: Play knight to f4, threatening knight to d3. If the opponent doesn't prevent it, execute the sacrifice to win the queen and simplify to a winning endgame.

notes.explains: When your opponent's pieces are poorly coordinated, you can often create forks. Here, a knight fork on rooks is a classic pattern that wins material.
notes.teaches: Always be on the lookout for knight forks, especially when the opponent's pieces are on the same colored squares or close together. Avoid moving your pieces into forking squares.
notes.plans: If the opponent blunders into a fork, take the material. If they avoid it, you still have a strong position.

notes.explains: When the queen and king are on the same diagonal or line, a bishop or knight can often fork them. Here the bishop on c5 would win the queen because of the alignment.
notes.teaches: Always be alert for forks and skewers involving the enemy king and queen. Look for pieces that can attack both at once.
